before: I set off downtown and east for the Delmonico rooms. It was a good walk. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ The Delmonico rooms over the fish market were up a steep stair from Catherine Street, three floors of them. The market below was shut and its stalls hosed down. But the smell of fish hadn’t gone anywhere. A framed sign in the hall said that baths were on Saturdays and the hot water was by arrangement. ¶ Mrs. Steinbach was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. ¶ Feeney had said Mrs. Steinbach was with her at Feeney’s place at nine. It was reason enough to look. ¶ There was nobody on duty, and nobody to ask who had been by.
card: The hall had a coat stand with nobody’s coat on it.

before: It was no distance to the alley at Steinmetz’s: round the corner, and there it was. The fog had come up off the river and was taking the streetlamps one at a time. ¶ The alley behind Steinmetz’s was ash cans and crates and a puddle that never dries, lit by the kitchen door when it opened and by nothing when it didn’t. Somebody had made a bench out of an oyster crate and a plank. The cobbles round it were thick with cigarette ends, where the kitchen does its thinking. There was the swinging door to the kitchen, with a porthole in it greased over so the dining room can’t see what goes into the chops. ¶ Kaminsky was eating a raw egg out of the shell, for the strength. He had hands taped at the knuckles out of habit, and a smile with a gap in it that he keeps for photographs. ¶ He had been at Glick’s at eight, for the meeting. That was reason enough. ¶ It was the kind of place nobody kept an eye on.
card: Nobody offered to take my hat. I hadn’t expected anybody to.

before: Brennan’s flat lay a good walk uptown and east. A newspaper went by in the gutter, and it might have been the same one. It was making better time than I was. ¶ I went back to Brennan’s flat, because there’s no such thing as a place you’re finished with. ¶ Brennan was at the sink with her sleeves rolled up, and dried her hands slowly before she turned round. ¶ Shapiro had said she was with him at the Tramonti flat at eight. It was reason enough to look.
card: The hall had a coat stand with nobody’s coat on it.

before: Kowalski’s was only round the corner, which I wrote down: the whole night was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ I went to Mrs. Kowalski’s boarding house on Orchard Street. It was a narrow brick house with a scrubbed stoop and a smell of beet soup that had got into the walls and settled. The stair had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Kowalski sat in the open door of the front room with a basket of mending, where the stair was never out of sight. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. ¶ The revolver had come from here. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. Nobody comes or goes in a rooming house without the landlady knowing, and Mrs. Kowalski had the look of a landlady who made a point of it.
card: I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

before: It was a few blocks from there to the costume room at the Lyric, uptown and west, with my collar up. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ The costume room under the Lyric’s stage was racks and racks of other people: peasants and rabbis, a czar, three brides and a dragon in two halves. A sewing machine stood under the only light with a wedding dress half mended across it, beside a box of buttons and a cold glass of tea. There was a pair of silver candlesticks for the Sabbath scene in the second act, real silver, counted by the stage manager before the curtain and after. ¶ Lieb, with a cane, was eating peanuts out of his hat, and he had a silk scarf with somebody else’s monogram on it, worn with the monogram tucked in. ¶ Dr. Hirsch had said he was with her at the Kaminsky flat at eight. It was a thread. I meant to pull it. ¶ Anybody could have come and gone, and nobody would have known it.
card: It was warmer in than out, which was the best thing I could say for it. I said it.
place: the costume room at the Lyric

before: The chop house was a fair few blocks downtown, near enough for anybody to walk it there and back inside the hour. I made a note of that. The cold had got into the gutters, and the gutters had given up. ¶ I went into the Grand Street chop house. It was dark wood and white tablecloths, with the grill at the back cooling down and ticking to itself. The day’s specials were chalked on a slate by the door, and the soup had been crossed out. ¶ Prentiss, the head waiter, was standing by the coats with a menu under his arm, in case anybody wanted one at this hour. Steinbach was at a corner table with a plate of toast, eating it slowly, a corner at a time, like somebody paying by the bite. She was neat in a way that took effort: every button done, the collar pinned, the hair flat. The hands stayed folded until she needed one, and then only the one. ¶ A head waiter shows everybody to a table, so Prentiss would know who had come in tonight and where they’d been put.
card: The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

before: The Lyric was only round the corner, and I was there before I’d finished a thought. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ The Lyric had emptied as far as a theater ever empties, which isn’t far: programs on the seats, somebody’s glove, a bag of sunflower seeds spilled in the twelfth row. Up in the ventilator over the gallery, the pigeons were rehearsing. There was a poster in the lobby, THE RABBI’S DAUGHTER, ELEVENTH TRIUMPHANT WEEK, with ‘and twelfth’ added in pencil. ¶ Pinsky was waxing the points of his mustache with a licked finger, and he had a white mustache waxed to points so fine they quiver when he disapproves. Mrs. Blau was touching a lace handkerchief to her temples. As if somebody were calling. Miss Moskin was eating a knish in full costume. ¶ Mrs. Krantz had said she was here at nine, with Miss Moskin. It was reason enough to look. ¶ From his post he could see the whole house, from the back of the center aisle. “From the back of the aisle I see the back of every head in the place, and the back of a head tells you more than a face: who leans, who doesn’t laugh, who keeps turning round to look at the doors.”
card: Nobody offered to take my hat. I hadn’t expected anybody to.

before: The flats over Lipsky’s were only round the corner, and I was there before I’d finished a thought. The moon had moved along a few roofs since the last time I looked. It kept better hours than I did. ¶ The flats over Lipsky’s were waking from the top down, a light on the fifth floor, then the fourth. In the street the first pushcart man was already untying his tarpaulin. In the cloth shop’s window a dressmaker’s dummy wore a hat it had been wearing since spring, and wore it well. The janitor knocks his pipe out on the stoop rail so often the rail has a dent in it the shape of the bowl. ¶ Wojcik was knocking his pipe out on his boot heel and looking at nothing. He had coal dust in the creases of his knuckles that no soap on Orchard Street has ever got out. Amato was jingling the change in his pocket like a meter running. Mrs. Sobel was complaining to the janitor through the radiator. ¶ Margolis had said he was here at eight, and that Amato was with him at Margolis’s place at eight, and that was worth the walk. From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “The stoop has five steps, and the fourth one rings when you stand on it. I don’t fix it.”
card: The place smelled of soap and supper and somebody’s good intentions.

before: I set off east for Kaminsky’s place. It was a few blocks. The first light was coming up over the river, thin and gray, and the streetlamps hadn’t heard about it yet. ¶ Kaminsky’s place looked the same the second time, which in my line of work is never quite true. ¶ Amato let me in and then stayed in the hall, the way people do when they don’t want to look at a room. ¶ Kaminsky had died here. It was reason enough to look.
card: A clock in the hall was keeping time for nobody in particular.

before: Moskowitz’s lay a few blocks uptown and west. Second Avenue was running with water, curb to curb. ¶ I went down to Moskowitz’s, a Romanian restaurant four steps down on Second Avenue. The place smelled of garlic and grilled meat, there was a basket of bread on every table, and the piano in the corner had a cloth over it for the night. A big samovar sat at the end of the counter, steaming quietly to itself. ¶ Callahan stood by the reservation book at the door with a pencil, crossing out tables nobody would want now. Ashby, in a camel coat, was finishing a plate of something with the care of somebody who had paid for it. Young and tidy and a little tired, he still had the mark of the headset band pressed into his hair. ¶ Dettweiler had been here earlier in the evening. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ Nobody sits down in a restaurant without the head waiter deciding where, and Callahan had been doing the deciding.
card: Nobody offered to take my hat. I hadn’t expected anybody to.

before: From there to the Orpheum was a couple of blocks, and it was raining the steady kind of rain that has nowhere else to be. ¶ I let myself back into the Orpheum, and nobody made a fuss about it. ¶ Bellucci stood at the back of the house with a flashlight, pointed at the floor, ready. Lanza, in a green hat, was in the back row with a bag of peanuts, shelling them one at a time and not eating them.
card: The empty seats went back into the dark, row on row, all of them paying attention.

before: Sokol’s lay a couple of blocks west. The doorways along here were full of people waiting out the rain. Nobody offered to share. ¶ The bar behind Sokol’s bakery was shut, which there means the chairs were up and the barman was still at it, drying glasses and counting them onto a towel. In the front the ovens were coming back up for the morning. The whole place smelled of yeast and gin, which is the smell of a man with two jobs and no sleep. There was a bread knife on the bakery counter as long as a man’s forearm, kept sharp enough to slice a roll without waking it. ¶ Sokol was wiping flour off the gin bottles. He had eyes red at the rims from being up since four, every day, for nineteen years. Mrs. Pomerantz was looking at a stranger’s hair as if pricing it. Mabry was tapping out a tempo on the table with two fingers. Dr. Hirsch was reading a journal with her spectacles pushed up on her forehead. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty’s list had Mabry at Rafferty’s at eight and nine, and Dr. Hirsch at eight, nine and ten, and that was worth the walk. From his post Sokol could see the bar, the four tables and the door through from the bakery. “I count glasses. Every glass that goes out comes back, and I know whose hand it came back in.”
card: The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

before: Sokol’s was a couple of blocks uptown and west, near enough for anybody to walk it there and back inside the hour. I made a note of that. A dance hall upstairs was letting out, and the street was full of people saying goodnight at length. ¶ Sokol’s sold bread at the front and gin at the back. After midnight you went through the dark bakery, past ovens still warm and racks of tomorrow’s rolls rising under cloths, to a door with FLOUR painted on it. Behind the door were six stools, four tables and a radio playing dance music low, so it wouldn’t get into the bread. The barman counts the glasses onto a towel at closing, and when one is short he knows whose it was. ¶ Sokol was counting glasses onto a towel. He had eyes red at the rims from being up since four, every day, for nineteen years. Mrs. Pomerantz was taking a pin out of her mouth to say something and putting it back instead. ¶ Dr. Hirsch had sat here telling the room about her parlor window. That settled where I was going. From his post he could see the bar, the four tables and the door through from the bakery. “I count glasses. Every glass that goes out comes back, and I know whose hand it came back in.”
card: The smoke hung under the lamps in layers, as if the room were saving it for later.

before: The Velvet Room was a fair few blocks downtown and west. A trolley went by with three people on it, all of them asleep, and the conductor looking as if he’d like to be. ¶ I went down to the Velvet Room, six steps down under a hat shop. Upstairs the hat shop had gone dark, and down here the lamps were low and the talk was lower, the way it gets after midnight when the loud things have all been said. A brass spittoon stood at the foot of the bar, polished brighter than anything else in the room. ¶ Crowninshield was polishing a glass that was already clean, which is what bartenders do instead of watching you. She had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Stannard, with a cane, was at the bar with a drink she wasn’t drinking. ¶ Hargrove had said he was here at ten and eleven, and that she was with him at the Obermann flat at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ From behind a bar you can see the whole room and the door, and that side of the bar belonged to Crowninshield.
card: I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

before: A few blocks west, and I was at the Lyric. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ The Lyric had emptied as far as a theater ever empties, which isn’t far: programs on the seats, somebody’s glove, a bag of sunflower seeds spilled in the twelfth row. Up in the ventilator over the gallery, the pigeons were rehearsing. There was a pair of silver candlesticks for the Sabbath scene in the second act, real silver, counted by the stage manager before the curtain and after. ¶ Pinsky was sweeping sunflower shells out of the gallery, and he had his seating chart under one arm on a clipboard, the way other men carry a newspaper. Margolis was listening to an engine nobody else could hear. Miss Kahane was handing a leaflet to somebody who already had two. Glick was polishing his derby with his sleeve. ¶ Mrs. Sobel had said she was here at eight, and that Margolis was with her at her place at seven. It was reason enough to look. ¶ From his post Pinsky could see the whole house, from the back of the center aisle. “I seat by the chart. Every seat sold is a cross, every cross has a face, and I could draw you the face.”
card: The seats were all turned the same way, waiting for something. I knew how they felt.

before: The Odessa lay a couple of blocks downtown. The fog was still at the end of whatever street I was on. It followed me better than I follow people. ¶ I went to the Odessa, a café where the actors eat after the show. The tables were marble, the tea came in glasses, and the mirrors on every wall made the room look three times the size it was. A big samovar sat at the end of the counter, steaming quietly to itself. ¶ Whitfield was perched on a high stool behind the register, with a cigar box of change and a spike of paid bills. Feeney sat with his coat on and his plate pushed away, finishing a glass of seltzer. Young and tidy and a little tired, he still had the mark of the headset band pressed into his hair. Moretti sat at a table near the kitchen door with a newspaper folded to the crossword and a cup of coffee going cold. Sweeney had a table by the window and a glass of tea gone cold. ¶ Whitfield sits at the register, and sooner or later the whole room has to come to her.
card: I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

before: I set off east for the Russo flat. It was a couple of blocks. The moon was out and doing a thorough job of it, every railing and every step picked out in white. ¶ Back at the Russo flat. Nothing had moved but the clock. ¶ Russo, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ The watch had gone from here. I wanted another look before anybody tidied up.
card: The stairs had opinions about my weight and shared them all the way up.

before: Getting to the Greco flat meant a couple of blocks east, and the fog was going gray at the top, which was how I knew the morning had started without me. ¶ The Greco flat again, a little later and a little quieter. ¶ Mrs. Greco, my client, had beaten me there and was waiting on the landing, with her coat on and her hands in her pockets. ¶ Before I asked anybody anything more, I wanted another look at where Caruso had been.
card: I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

before: The Peacock was a fair few blocks uptown and west, near enough for anybody to walk it there and back inside the hour. I made a note of that. The first light was coming up over the river, thin and gray, and the streetlamps hadn’t heard about it yet. ¶ The Peacock again. The welcome was about what it had been the first time. ¶ Mrs. Szabo was on a chair tipped back against the door frame, chewing a toothpick down to splinters. Mrs. Krantz, in a green hat, was at the bar with her back to the room, watching the room in the mirror.
card: My feet were glad to stop, and said so.

before: A fair few blocks uptown and west, and I was at the Peacock. The street was as empty as a street gets, which in this city is never quite empty. ¶ Down in the cellar club it was the last set, for the serious drinkers, and the band had slowed to match them. Smoke hung under the low ceiling like a second ceiling. Through the velvet curtain at the foot of the stairs, four couples on the dance floor were holding each other up. There was an ice pick on the bar beside the block of ice they chip for highballs, with tape wound round the handle for a better grip. ¶ Mrs. Szabo was explaining to a large man why he was going home, and she had big hands folded in her lap, the knuckles flattened by a career she doesn’t discuss. Mrs. Krantz was writing in a rent book with a fountain pen. Teitel was folding a necktie into a pocket square for a man who hadn’t asked. ¶ From her post Mrs. Szabo could see the street door through the slot, and the stairs down. “There’s one way in and one way out, and I’m sitting in both of them.”
card: I found a place at the bar and let the room settle around me.

before: It was a fair few blocks to Feldman’s place, uptown and west. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. I wondered if the cab driver was still asleep at the curb. Somebody in this city ought to be. ¶ Feldman’s place looked the same the second time, which in my line of work is never quite true. ¶ Feeney had got there before me and looked up when I came in, the way people look up when they’re paying for your time. ¶ This was where Feldman had died. Everything else would be somebody’s story, and the room wouldn’t.
card: I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

before: The Kit Kat was only round the corner, which I wrote down: the whole night was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ I went up the outside stair to the Kit Kat, a speakeasy over a garage. The garage underneath was shut for the night, but the room still smelled of motor oil under the perfume and the cigarettes. A glass globe hung from the ceiling with half its little mirrors gone, turning slowly over the dance floor. ¶ Feeney was on a stool by the door with a newspaper he wasn’t reading. Heavy in the coat and light on his feet, he had the door swung wide before I’d reached for it, and shut again before I’d decided anything. Tillman was at the bar with his back to the room, watching the room in the mirror. Lanza sat at the end of the long bench by the wall, with a glass of ginger ale and a very straight back. Feldman was by the bandstand, picking out a tune with one finger on the band’s piano. ¶ Steinbach had sat here telling the room about her parlor window. That settled where I was going. ¶ Everybody who came in tonight had to get past Feeney first, and he has the kind of face that remembers who tried.
card: I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

before: I went round the corner to the plaster room at the back at Dr. Hirsch’s surgery. The stars were out over the rooftops, which in this city means somebody forgot to switch something on. ¶ The plaster room at the back of the surgery was a narrow room with a sink, a workbench white with dust and a shelf of plaster jaws in rows, every one of them grinning. A set of new teeth for somebody was drying on a sheet of newspaper, smiling up at the ceiling. A wooden chair with one short leg stood by the wall, and rocked whenever anything touched it. ¶ Kaminsky was shadowboxing in a corner, very quietly, so as not to bother anybody. He had hands taped at the knuckles out of habit, and a smile with a gap in it that he keeps for photographs. ¶ Miss Kahane had pointed me at him, and that was worth the walk. ¶ Nobody kept watch there. It wasn’t that kind of place.
card: It was the sort of room people say they were never in. I made a note that I was.
place: the plaster room at the back at Dr. Hirsch’s surgery

before: From there to Bellucci’s place was a few blocks. I thought about the watchman at his barrel. A fire and nothing to do but mind it. Some people have all the luck. ¶ Back at Bellucci’s place, everything was where I’d left it except the time. ¶ Salerno let me in and then stayed in the hall, the way people do when they don’t want to look at a room. ¶ A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and that was worth the walk.
card: I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

before: The Abramowitz flat was a fair few blocks downtown and east. A coal cart was making its first round, and the man on it had a scarf wound up to his eyes and no intention of talking. ¶ Back at the Abramowitz flat, everything was where I’d left it except the time. ¶ Abramowitz let me in and then stayed in the hall, the way people do when they don’t want to look at a room. ¶ He had said the watch went from here, and a place is the one witness that stays put.
card: I stood a moment and let my eyes catch up with the rest of me.

before: I went round the corner to Wexler’s. Steam came up out of the street gratings, the only warm thing on the block, and a row of pigeons was sitting on one with their eyes shut. ¶ Every overcoat on the Bowery seemed to be in the pawnshop window, pledged in summer by men who believed it would stay summer, each with its ticket pinned to the lapel, and the men somewhere outside in the cold. Inside, the cage had a little stove in it, for the pawnbroker, and the shop had none, for the customers. There was the back room, where the unredeemed coats hang in rows, and a tuba and a barber’s chair share a corner with the clerk’s cot. ¶ Wexler was looking at a coat’s lining before its outside. He had fingertips stained gray from tickets and newsprint and other people’s silver. ¶ Mrs. Greco had said she was here at nine. That was reason enough. ¶ From his post he could see the shop and the street door, from behind his cage. “I look at what a man brings before I look at the man. A ring tells me he’s married, a watch tells me he’s desperate, and a coat tells me if he’s coming back for it.”
card: I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

before: I walked downtown and east to Kaplan’s pawnshop. It was a couple of blocks, and I took all of it. The street was empty and clear and very quiet, and my heels were the loudest thing on it. ¶ Kaplan’s pawnshop on the Bowery was shut, with the grille pulled across the window and a light on somewhere at the back. Everything in a pawnshop is waiting for somebody to come back for it, and mostly nobody does. A brass scale with a set of little weights stood at one end of the counter, perfectly balanced. ¶ Shapiro was tidying the shelves behind the counter, turning every label to face the front. A jeweler’s glass hung on a ribbon round his neck, and he had a habit of turning things upside down to see the bottom. ¶ Coffin had said she was here at eight. That settled where I was going. ¶ A shopkeeper knows every customer by what they came in for, and Shapiro knew most of them by what they owed.
card: The place had that after-hours smell of work done and work waiting.

before: I walked east to Rafferty’s. It was a couple of blocks, and I took all of it. The fog had come up off the river and was taking the streetlamps one at a time. ¶ The milk wagon was two streets off and I could hear every bottle on it, which tells you how quiet the rooming house had got. The hall smelled of soda bread and floor polish; the landlady polishes before she sleeps, so the morning finds it done. Every door upstairs had a brass number on it, and every number shone. There was the late Mr. Rafferty’s revolver, in the hall-stand drawer under the winter gloves, unloaded, she says, which is what everybody says. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was writing in the rent book in pencil and going over it in ink. She had a ring of keys at her belt the size of a saucer, and she knows each key by the sound it makes. ¶ From her post she could see the front door, the stairs and every landing to the top. “I sit on the first landing with the mending till the last one’s in, and nobody gets up my stairs without stepping over the basket.”
card: Nobody offered to take my hat. I hadn’t expected anybody to.

before: It was no distance to the Eagle club office: round the corner, and there it was. A man was hosing down the sidewalk outside a lunch room, and he moved the hose politely to let me by. ¶ I went through to the back office of the Eagle Social Club. It was a small room with a roll-top desk, a framed portrait of somebody important and a big iron safe with the club’s eagle painted on the door. An old radiator by the wall gave off a great deal more noise than heat. ¶ Petrosino had a chair in the corner and a cup of coffee, and the look of somebody who would say he was only passing. ¶ Anybody could have come and gone, and nobody would have known it.
card: The room had been arranged so that nobody in it was ever quite facing anybody else.

before: Dettweiler’s flat was only round the corner, and I was there before I’d finished a thought. A milkman was leaving bottles on the steps, two by two, as quietly as a man can do anything with glass. ¶ I went round to Dettweiler’s flat on Suffolk Street. It was a walk-up like every walk-up on Suffolk Street: a hall that smelled of other people’s suppers and a stair with a bend in it. A kettle sat on a gas ring on the shelf, gone cold. ¶ Dettweiler was at the window with the curtain held back an inch, keeping an eye on the street. He was neat in a way that took effort: every button done, the collar pinned, the hair flat. The hands stayed folded until he needed one, and then only the one. ¶ It was the kind of place nobody kept an eye on.
card: I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

before: Rafferty’s was a good walk uptown and west, and I took it at a good clip. Steam came up out of the street gratings, the only warm thing on the block, and a row of pigeons was sitting on one with their eyes shut. ¶ I went up the stoop at Rafferty’s rooming house on Mott Street. It was four floors of narrow rooms and one long stair, with a gas lamp on each landing turned down to a little blue bead. The stair had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Lanza was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. ¶ Weisglass had said Mrs. Lanza minded Caruso when Weisglass was out. That was reason enough for the walk. It was the kind of place nobody kept an eye on.
card: I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

before: The Eagle club office lay a good walk uptown and west. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ I went through to the back office of the Eagle Social Club. It was a small room with a roll-top desk, a framed portrait of somebody important and a big iron safe with the club’s eagle painted on the door. An old radiator by the wall gave off a great deal more noise than heat. ¶ Rosenbaum, in a fur collar, was sitting where she could see the door, with her hat on and her coat buttoned. She had fingertips gone flat from typing all day, and was dressed for an office in a good plain way that no office would ever notice. ¶ Vogel had said Rosenbaum was with her at the Colquitt flat at eight. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had.
card: I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

before: Moskowitz’s was a few blocks uptown and east, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ I went down to Moskowitz’s, a Romanian restaurant four steps down on Second Avenue. The place smelled of garlic and grilled meat, there was a basket of bread on every table, and the piano in the corner had a cloth over it for the night. A big samovar sat at the end of the counter, steaming quietly to itself. ¶ Bledsoe, the head waiter, was standing by the coats with a menu under her arm, in case anybody wanted one at this hour. Kreuzer had a table by the window and a glass of tea gone cold. Round and pleasant and dressed a little too well for a cigar store, he kept his eyes on the door, in case it was the police or a winner. Stannard sat at a table by the mirror with a glass of tea, drinking it the old way, through a lump of sugar held in her teeth. ¶ Bellucci had been here earlier in the evening. That settled where I was going. ¶ Bledsoe seats everybody who comes in, and a good head waiter never forgets a customer, least of all one who didn’t tip.
card: I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

before: The Thalia was only round the corner, and I was there before I’d finished a thought. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ I went in at the Thalia, a Yiddish theater on the Bowery. The play was over, but the stage still had its painted village up, a little wooden town waiting under one work light for the next performance. A big brass ashtray full of sand stood by the inner doors, with a neat pattern raked into the sand. ¶ Rosenbaum stood at the back of the house with a flashlight, pointed at the floor, ready. Vitale was in the back row with a bag of peanuts, shelling them one at a time and not eating them. Young and tidy and a little tired, he still had the mark of the headset band pressed into his hair. Sweeney stood at the back with his hat in his hand, as if he had just come in or was just going. ¶ Kessler had said she was here at nine, with him. That settled where I was going. ¶ Nobody gets into a theater without going past the front of the house, and the front of the house was Rosenbaum.
card: The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

before: A couple of blocks east, and I was at the flats over Lipsky’s. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ The flats over Lipsky’s were waking from the top down, a light on the fifth floor, then the fourth. In the street the first pushcart man was already untying his tarpaulin. In the cloth shop’s window a dressmaker’s dummy wore a hat it had been wearing since spring, and wore it well. There was a row of tin mailboxes in the hall, with the names in five different hands and two crossed out. ¶ Wojcik was answering the fourth floor by banging a pipe with a wrench. He had coal dust in the creases of his knuckles that no soap on Orchard Street has ever got out. Amato was jingling the change in his pocket like a meter running. Mrs. Sobel was drinking tea from a glass with a lump of sugar in her teeth. ¶ From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “I know the tenants by their shoes. Faces, I don’t look at. A face can lie. A shoe has been where it’s been.”
card: The hall had a coat stand with nobody’s coat on it.

before: It was a few blocks to Whitfield’s place, downtown and west, and the cold was still out there doing its rounds. It’s the only thing in this city that works all night for nothing. ¶ I let myself back into Whitfield’s place, and nobody made a fuss about it. ¶ Hauck let me in and then stayed in the hall, the way people do when they don’t want to look at a room. ¶ The night had started here, with Whitfield, and I wanted to see it again with what I knew now.
card: The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

before: From there to Steinmetz’s was a couple of blocks. The rain had the street to itself and was making the most of it. ¶ Closing a chop house of the old kind takes an hour, and Steinmetz’s was in the middle of it: the chairs going up table by table, slowly, so as not to hurry anybody who might still order pie. The head waiter stood at his stand by the door, writing the last covers in his book in ink. The sawdust had been swept into the corners to think over what it had heard, and there was an umbrella stand made from an elephant’s foot. Which the owner swears is a cow’s. ¶ Demos was holding a fork up to the light. He had a white napkin over one forearm even off duty. He says he feels undressed without it. Russo, with a bandaged hand, was sitting with his back to the wall. ¶ Miss Nowak had said she was here at seven, and that he was with her at her place at eight. It was reason enough to look. ¶ From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “A gentleman orders the chop, sir. A man with something on his mind orders the soup. A man with something worse orders nothing and asks for the check.”
card: The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

before: From there to the Lyric was a few blocks. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ The Lyric had emptied as far as a theater ever empties, which isn’t far: programs on the seats, somebody’s glove, a bag of sunflower seeds spilled in the twelfth row. Up in the ventilator over the gallery, the pigeons were rehearsing. There was the usher’s seating chart on a clipboard, every seat sold a pencil cross. ¶ Pinsky was marking crosses on his seating chart. He had his seating chart under one arm on a clipboard. The way other men carry a newspaper. Mrs. Krantz was counting bills with a rubber thumb. Kaminsky was eating a raw egg out of the shell, for the strength. ¶ Mrs. Sobel had said Mrs. Krantz was with her at Mrs. Sobel’s place at ten. That was reason enough. ¶ From his post Pinsky could see the whole house, from the back of the center aisle. “From the back of the aisle I see the back of every head in the place, and the back of a head tells you more than a face: who leans, who doesn’t laugh, who keeps turning round to look at the doors.”
card: Somebody had left a program on a seat, and I didn’t read it. I had enough people to keep track of.

before: It was a few blocks to Moe’s, uptown and east. The moon had moved along a few roofs since the last time I looked. It kept better hours than I did. ¶ Moe’s, a back-room bar behind a cigar store, was one room with no windows, a curtain for a door and a bar along one wall. After midnight it had the quiet of a place that expects to be quiet and is paid to be. A brass spittoon stood at the foot of the bar, polished brighter than anything else in the room. ¶ Vitale was behind the bar with both hands spread on it, the way somebody stands who has been standing since the afternoon and has opinions about it. She had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Mosley was on a stool with her hat pushed back, turning a coin over and over on the bar. Moretti had a stool at the end of the bar and was looking at the mirror behind it, which looked back. Steinbach was at the far end of the bar, reading the racing page and making little marks beside the horses. ¶ From behind a bar you can see the whole room and the door, and that side of the bar belonged to Vitale.
card: The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

before: I went round the corner to Sokol’s. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ The bar behind Sokol’s bakery was shut, which there means the chairs were up and the barman was still at it, drying glasses and counting them onto a towel. In the front the ovens were coming back up for the morning. The whole place smelled of yeast and gin, which is the smell of a man with two jobs and no sleep. There was a radio on the shelf behind the bar, turned low so the music won’t get into the bread. ¶ Sokol was rubbing his eyes with the heels of both hands, like a man trying to put them back. He had a row of old burns across the back of one hand, in stripes, from an oven rack that got him in 1911. Mrs. Pomerantz was taking a pin out of her mouth to say something and putting it back instead. Mabry was tapping out a tempo on the table with two fingers. ¶ From his post Sokol could see the bar, the four tables and the door through from the bakery. “I don’t look up when the door goes. I look up when it doesn’t, because then somebody is standing in it deciding.”
card: The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

before: Moe’s was a couple of blocks uptown. Rivington Street was running with water, curb to curb. ¶ Moe’s looked the same the second time. Which in my line of work is never quite true. ¶ Mulcahy was behind the bar, setting clean glasses upside down in rows on a towel. Petrosino, in a grey fedora, was on a stool with his hat pushed back, turning a coin over and over on the bar.
card: Somebody laughed at the far end of the bar. It wasn’t at me, for once.

before: From there to the Lyric was a few blocks. The moon was out and doing a thorough job of it, every railing and every step picked out in white. ¶ The Lyric was a Yiddish playhouse on Second Avenue, all gold paint and red plush, with clouds on the ceiling touched up by somebody who had never seen a cloud. After midnight the house lights were down and one work light stood on the stage among the scenery for the third act: a rabbi’s study, with books painted on the shelves and one real chair. There was the usher’s seating chart on a clipboard, every seat sold a pencil cross. ¶ Pinsky was pointing his flashlight at a man who was talking. He had a white mustache waxed to points so fine they quiver when he disapproves. Miss Nowak was counting out change for a horse she likes. Miss Lowenthal was listening to the orchestra with her eyes closed and her mouth disapproving. Doyle was shaking hands with a man who didn’t offer his. ¶ Miss Kahane had pointed me at Miss Lowenthal, who asked twice whether Duchess had papers at the christening supper, and that was worth the walk. ¶ From his post Pinsky could see the whole house, from the back of the center aisle. “I seat by the chart. Every seat sold is a cross, every cross has a face, and I could draw you the face.”
card: Somebody had left a program on a seat, and I didn’t read it. I had enough people to keep track of.

before: From there to Steinmetz’s was a couple of blocks. A dance hall upstairs was letting out, and the street was full of people saying goodnight at length. ¶ Steinmetz’s had its name in gold on the window, CHOPS STEAKS OYSTERS, lit from below by the lamps on the oyster bar, and behind it a long room going quietly about the last orders of the night. The waiters wore white aprons to the ankle, which made them look as if they were standing in buckets, and the tables near the door were already stripped to the wood. There was an umbrella stand made from an elephant’s foot, which the owner swears is a cow’s. ¶ Demos was holding a fork up to the light, and he had a white napkin over one forearm even off duty. He says he feels undressed without it. Mrs. Blau was staring at a spot just over a stranger’s left shoulder. Miss Nowak was counting out change for a horse she likes. Miss Kahane was counting union dues into a cocoa tin. ¶ Belkin had pointed me at Miss Nowak, who picked Mimi up and asked what Mimi cost at the supper, and that was worth the walk. From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “I seat every table myself, and I write the covers in the book with the time beside them. Nobody sits in my room without my say-so.”
card: I took a seat where I could see the door, which is the only habit of mine that ever paid.

before: It was a fair few blocks to the Russo flat, downtown and east. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ The Russo flat looked the same the second time, which in my line of work is never quite true. ¶ Russo, my client, had beaten me there and was waiting on the landing, with his coat on and his hands in his pockets. ¶ Before I asked anybody anything more, I wanted another look at where Duchess had been.
card: I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

before: The Russo flat was a few blocks downtown, near enough for anybody to walk it there and back inside the hour. I made a note of that. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ Back at the Russo flat, everything was where I’d left it except the time. ¶ Russo had got there before me and looked up when I came in, the way people look up when they’re paying for your time. ¶ This was where Mimi had been and wasn’t any more, and I wanted another look.
card: I stood a moment and let my eyes catch up with the rest of me.

before: From there to the Peacock was a few blocks. My shoes had let the rain in two blocks back, and now they were just carrying it around for me. ¶ Down in the cellar club it was the last set, for the serious drinkers, and the band had slowed to match them. Smoke hung under the low ceiling like a second ceiling. Through the velvet curtain at the foot of the stairs, four couples on the dance floor were holding each other up. There was the smell of lilies coming down through the floorboards from the undertaker’s, which the gin covers until about one. ¶ Mrs. Szabo was looking through the slot in the steel door. She had big hands folded in her lap, the knuckles flattened by a career she doesn’t discuss. Miss Kahane, in a grey fedora, was counting union dues into a cocoa tin. ¶ Kaminsky had been here earlier in the evening. That was reason enough. From her post Mrs. Szabo could see the street door through the slot, and the stairs down. “Every face comes to my slot first. I don’t like most of them, so the ones I let in, I remember.”
card: The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

before: I walked it at an ordinary pace, uptown and west to the Peacock, a fair few blocks, and wrote it down. An hour only holds so many walks like that. The rain had the street to itself and was making the most of it. ¶ Down in the cellar club it was the last set, for the serious drinkers, and the band had slowed to match them. Smoke hung under the low ceiling like a second ceiling. Through the velvet curtain at the foot of the stairs, four couples on the dance floor were holding each other up. There was the cigarette girl’s tray, Luckies and Camels on the top layer and, underneath, a layer nobody buys cigarettes from. ¶ Mrs. Szabo was cracking her knuckles one at a time, in order, and she had big hands folded in her lap, the knuckles flattened by a career she doesn’t discuss. Mrs. Blau was staring at a spot just over a stranger’s left shoulder. Mrs. Krantz was drinking lemon tea with the lemon left in. ¶ From her post Mrs. Szabo could see the street door through the slot, and the stairs down. “I listen to the knock before I open the slot. A friend knocks twice and waits. A policeman knocks like he owns the door. A man with something to hide knocks once and starts talking.”
card: The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

before: Glick’s place was a few blocks east, and I took it at a good clip. The rain was letting up as the sky went gray, as if it had only come out to keep the night company. ¶ Glick’s place looked the same the second time, which in my line of work is never quite true. ¶ Mrs. Ostrow had got there before me and looked up when I came in, the way people look up when they’re paying for your time. ¶ A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him. That settled where I was going.
card: The hall had a coat stand with nobody’s coat on it.

before: It was a fair few blocks from there to the Blue Lantern, uptown and west, with my collar up. Water ran down the gutters in a hurry, carrying a newspaper with it. ¶ The Blue Lantern, a cellar club behind a laundry, smelled faintly of starch, which is more than any other club in the city can say. The lantern over the bandstand was blue, as promised, and so was most of the music. A glass globe hung from the ceiling with half its little mirrors gone, turning slowly over the dance floor. ¶ Mulcahy was on a stool by the door with a newspaper she wasn’t reading. Heavy in the coat and light on her feet, she had the door swung wide before I’d reached for it, and shut again before I’d decided anything. Lathrop was at the bar with his back to the room, watching the room in the mirror. Reinhardt was by the bandstand, picking out a tune with one finger on the band’s piano. Steinbach sat at the end of the long bench by the wall, with a glass of ginger ale and a very straight back. ¶ Nobody gets into a place like this without Mulcahy looking them over first, and she looks people over for a living.
card: I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

before: I walked downtown and east to the Palace. It was a couple of blocks, and I took all of it. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ The back row of the Palace, a picture house on Delancey Street, was the darkest place on Delancey Street you could sit for a dime. That’s what the back row is for, and the management has known it for years. A bare bulb hung on a cord, swinging a little whenever the door shut. ¶ Fairbanks had a chair in the corner and a cup of coffee, and the look of somebody who would say she was only passing. ¶ Mulcahy had pointed me at her. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ Nobody kept a list of who came and went, on paper or in their head.
card: The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

before: Glick’s place was round the corner. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ Back at Glick’s place. Nothing had moved but the clock. ¶ Mrs. Ostrow was there, with a cup of something she hadn’t touched and her coat still buttoned. ¶ A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him. That settled where I was going.
card: I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

before: It was a couple of blocks from there to the Greco flat, downtown and east, with my collar up. A coal cart was making its first round, and the man on it had a scarf wound up to his eyes and no intention of talking. ¶ Back at the Greco flat, everything was where I’d left it except the time. ¶ Mrs. Greco had got there before me and looked up when I came in, the way people look up when they’re paying for your time. ¶ She had said Caruso went from here, and a place is the one witness that stays put.
card: Somebody’s radio was going behind a door, low, so as not to wake anybody who was already awake.

before: I headed downtown and east for Kaplan’s pawnshop, a few blocks away. Steam came up out of the street gratings, the only warm thing on the block, and a row of pigeons was sitting on one with their eyes shut. ¶ Kaplan’s pawnshop on the Bowery was shut, with the grille pulled across the window and a light on somewhere at the back. Everything in a pawnshop is waiting for somebody to come back for it, and mostly nobody does. A bell on a spring hung over the door, and it rang when I came in as if it had been waiting all day. ¶ Margolis was behind the counter, writing in a ledger by the light of a green-shaded lamp. A jeweler’s glass hung on a ribbon round her neck, and she had a habit of turning things upside down to see the bottom. ¶ Ainsworth had said she was here at nine. That was reason enough. ¶ Shut or not, nobody comes in at that door without Margolis looking up from behind the counter to see who it is.
card: I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

before: It was a fair few blocks to Weiss’s pharmacy, downtown and east. A man was hosing down the sidewalk outside a lunch room, and he moved the hose politely to let me by. ¶ Weiss’s pharmacy on Essex Street was shut, with a hand-lettered sign in the door saying to ring in an emergency. Every pharmacy has that sign. Every pharmacist hopes you won’t. A supply company’s calendar hung behind the counter, with every day crossed off in pencil. ¶ Lefkowitz was behind her counter in a gray coat, doing the day’s figures by the light of one lamp. Neat and gray and precise, she wrote everything down, and I had the feeling I’d be written down too before long. ¶ Reinhardt had said she was here at seven. That was reason enough for the walk. Whoever stands behind a counter all day sees everybody who comes to it. It’s what the counter is for.
card: I stood out of the way, which in a place like that is a job in itself.

before: Rafferty’s lay a couple of blocks uptown and west. A man was hosing down the sidewalk outside a lunch room, and he moved the hose politely to let me by. ¶ I went up the stoop at Rafferty’s rooming house on Mott Street. It was four floors of narrow rooms and one long stair, with a gas lamp on each landing turned down to a little blue bead. The stair had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was in the hall with a dustpan, sweeping a stair that had been swept already. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. ¶ She had her chair where nobody could get up the stairs without going round it, and I got the feeling nobody had ever tried twice.
card: I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

before: Getting to the undertaker’s cellar at the Peacock meant a few blocks uptown. The streetlamps went out all at once while I was under one, which felt personal. ¶ The undertaker’s cellar was through a coal hole in the Peacock’s back wall, into a long, cold, whitewashed room where the funeral parlor keeps what it keeps. There were trestles, a hand truck and a row of folding chairs for mourners, and the band came through the wall faint and cheerful. Like a party nobody down here had been asked to. There was a coffin on display in the undertaker’s window beside the stair, lid up, with the price folded on the pillow. ¶ Mabry was writing a tune on the back of an envelope. He had a callus on his upper lip from the cornet, which he touches when he’s thinking. ¶ Doyle had said he was here at ten. That was reason enough. Mabry had the room from the hour that mattered, and not before. Before that, he said, it was anybody’s.
card: There was one light. Everybody had arranged to be just outside it.
place: the undertaker’s cellar at the Peacock

before: Kaminsky’s flat lay a few blocks east. The fog was thick enough that I walked by the curb, one hand in my pocket and the other ready to apologize. ¶ By that hour the Belvedere had gone dark from the pickle store to the roof, every flat but one, where a kitchen light was on and a kettle was beginning to think about it. The stairs creaked under nobody at all, the way old stairs do at night, settling the day’s accounts. There was the street door’s lock, broken since Purim, and a loop of string over a nail that does the lock’s work for it. ¶ Kaminsky was skipping rope in the kitchen and ducking the light bulb on every turn. He had hands taped at the knuckles out of habit, and a smile with a gap in it that he keeps for photographs. ¶ Mrs. Szabo’s list had him at the Peacock at nine, and that was worth the walk. There was no one to notice who passed through.
card: I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

before: I set off downtown and west for the Delmonico rooms. It was a few blocks. The doorways along here were full of people waiting out the rain. Nobody offered to share. ¶ The Delmonico rooms over the fish market were up a steep stair from Catherine Street, three floors of them. The market below was shut and its stalls hosed down. But the smell of fish hadn’t gone anywhere. The stair had a brass rod on every step. One of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Hanrahan was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into her collar. ¶ Kessler had said she borrowed Duchess most evenings. That was reason enough. ¶ Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had.
card: I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

before: I set off west for the Automat. It was a fair few blocks. The streetlamps went out all at once while I was under one, which felt personal. ¶ I went into the Automat on Delancey Street, open all night. It was a long bright room of little glass doors, each with a sandwich or a slice of pie behind it, and a nickel would open any one of them. A bare bulb hung on a cord, swinging a little whenever the door shut. ¶ Cheatham was in the change booth, stacking nickels into columns of exactly twenty. ¶ Shapiro had said he was here at ten. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ Whoever sits in the change booth sees every hand that comes to the glass for nickels, and the faces above them.
card: The room had been arranged so that nobody in it was ever quite facing anybody else.

before: Steinmetz’s was a couple of blocks downtown and east, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. The cold had got into the gutters, and the gutters had given up. ¶ The front of Steinmetz’s was dark, but the kitchen door at the back stood propped open on the alley, letting out steam and the sound of a pot being scrubbed by somebody with opinions about it. The chop house window still said CHOPS STEAKS OYSTERS in gold, with the R gone from OYSTERS. There was an umbrella stand made from an elephant’s foot. Which the owner swears is a cow’s. ¶ Demos was writing covers in the book at his stand, and he had hair parted dead center and flattened with something that smells of violets. Miss Nowak was counting out change for a horse she likes. Miss Moskin was reading Variety for parts uptown. ¶ Russo had said he was here at eight, with Miss Nowak, and that was worth the walk. ¶ From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “A gentleman orders the chop, sir. A man with something on his mind orders the soup. A man with something worse orders nothing and asks for the check.”
card: Nobody offered to take my hat. I hadn’t expected anybody to.

before: I headed downtown and east for the Bijou, a good walk away. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ I went to the Bijou, a picture house on Clinton Street. It was a narrow little house with a ticket window the size of a mail slot and a smell of floor polish and oranges. A life-size cardboard cowboy stood in the lobby, fading, and tipping his hat at the box office. ¶ Broadnax was by the inner doors, sorting a stack of programs into the ones that could be used again and the ones that couldn’t. The uniform coat had the theater’s name on the collar, and the cap had been reshaped by a hundred hot nights. Whitfield sat in an aisle seat about halfway down, with his coat folded on his knees. Kessler stood at the back with his hat in his hand, as if he had just come in or was just going. ¶ Ellery had pointed me at Kessler. That was reason enough for the walk. An usher with a flashlight sees every face that comes in out of the street, and most of them twice.
card: The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

before: It was no distance to the flats over Lipsky’s: round the corner, and there it was. The cold had come down with the dark and meant to stay, and people were walking fast with their collars up and their opinions to themselves. ¶ The flats over Lipsky’s were five floors of brick on Orchard Street, with the cloth shop shut up at the bottom behind iron shutters. After midnight the pushcarts stood along the curb under their tarpaulins, waiting for morning. Down by the cellar steps under the stoop a pipe glowed and went dark: the janitor was still on his steps, or had left the pipe to do it for him. There was the roof door at the top of the stairs, propped open with a brick summer and winter, because nobody has told the brick it’s winter. ¶ Wojcik was eating a sandwich of black bread and onion out of a newspaper. He had a ring of keys on a bootlace round his neck, worn under his undershirt where nobody can borrow them. Mrs. Sobel was sitting in her kitchen doorway with her feet up on a crate. ¶ She had found Glick. That was reason enough. From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “I know the tenants by their shoes. Faces, I don’t look at. A face can lie. A shoe has been where it’s been.”
card: A clock in the hall was keeping time for nobody in particular.

before: Doyle’s place was a couple of blocks east. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ Back at Doyle’s place, I had my hands in my pockets and my questions in order. ¶ Dr. Hirsch had got there before me and looked up when I came in, the way people look up when they’re paying for your time. ¶ Doyle died here, so I looked again.
card: The place smelled of soap and supper and somebody’s good intentions.

before: A few blocks uptown and east, and I was at Moskowitz’s. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ I let myself back into Moskowitz’s, and nobody made a fuss about it. ¶ Feldman was going from table to table with a cloth over her arm, straightening chairs that were already straight. Lindemann, with a cane, sat at a table by the mirror with a glass of tea, drinking it the old way, through a lump of sugar held in his teeth.
card: I bought a coffee to look like I belonged. It cost a nickel. I got about a nickel’s worth.

before: It was a few blocks from there to the Thalia, downtown and west, with my collar up. Water ran down the gutters in a hurry, carrying a newspaper with it. ¶ The Thalia again, a little later and a little quieter. ¶ Lindemann, in a grey fedora, was in the back row with a bag of peanuts, shelling them one at a time and not eating them. Lanza was still there.
card: I looked the place over the way you read a bill: twice, and slowly.

before: It was a fair few blocks to the Shamrock, downtown and east. A man was hosing down the sidewalk outside a lunch room, and he moved the hose politely to let me by. ¶ I went into the Shamrock, a bar on the corner. It was a long narrow room with a brass rail worn bright where the feet go, and at this hour most of the feet had gone home. A brass spittoon stood at the foot of the bar, polished brighter than anything else in the room. ¶ Renfro was behind the bar with both hands spread on it, the way somebody stands who has been standing since the afternoon and has opinions about it. She had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Zeldin was standing at the bar with his coat over his arm, drinking something brown in small careful sips. ¶ A bartender who stands behind a bar all night knows who drank at it.
