before: The Shamrock was a fair few blocks downtown, and I took it at a good clip. Somewhere a radio was still arguing. It had been at it all night and hadn’t won yet. ¶ The Shamrock, a bar on the corner, had its windows painted green up to the height of a hat, so that Avenue B could see the lights were on and nothing else. Inside it smelled of beer and a radiator working harder than it was paid to. There was a radio on a shelf behind the bar, playing dance music so softly it might have been coming from next door. ¶ Brauer was behind the bar, setting clean glasses upside down in rows on a towel. She had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Tramonti was standing at the bar with his coat over his arm, drinking something brown in small careful sips. ¶ A bartender who stands behind a bar all night knows who drank at it.
card: I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

before: The Shamrock was a good walk downtown and east, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. The cold had got into the gutters, and the gutters had given up. ¶ I went into the Shamrock, a bar on the corner. It was a long narrow room with a brass rail worn bright where the feet go, and at this hour most of the feet had gone home. A brass spittoon stood at the foot of the bar, polished brighter than anything else in the room. ¶ Weisglass was behind the bar, setting clean glasses upside down in rows on a towel. She had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Colquitt was on a stool with her hat pushed back, turning a coin over and over on the bar. Tillman had a stool at the end of the bar and was looking at the mirror behind it, which looked back. ¶ Steinbach had said she was here at eight, with Colquitt. That settled where I was going. If anybody came in tonight, Weisglass poured for them, and she doesn’t pour for people she hasn’t looked at.
card: I found a place at the bar and let the room settle around me.

before: It was a couple of blocks to the Bijou, uptown and east. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ I went to the Bijou, a picture house on Clinton Street. It was a narrow little house with a ticket window the size of a mail slot and a smell of floor polish and oranges. A life-size cardboard cowboy stood in the lobby, fading, and tipping his hat at the box office. ¶ Colquitt was in the lobby, counting the evening’s ticket stubs into bundles and putting a rubber band round each one. The uniform coat had the theater’s name on the collar, and the cap had been reshaped by a hundred hot nights. Tramonti stood at the back with her hat in her hand, as if she had just come in or was just going. Steinbach sat in an aisle seat about halfway down, with her coat folded on her knees. ¶ Sirkin had said he was here at eight, and that Tramonti was with him at his place at seven, and that was worth the walk. Nobody gets into a theater without going past the front of the house, and the front of the house was Colquitt.
card: I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

before: Getting to Steinmetz’s meant a couple of blocks downtown and east. The cold had got into the gutters, and the gutters had given up. ¶ The front of Steinmetz’s was dark, but the kitchen door at the back stood propped open on the alley, letting out steam and the sound of a pot being scrubbed by somebody with opinions about it. The chop house window still said CHOPS STEAKS OYSTERS in gold, with the R gone from OYSTERS. There was sawdust on the floor, fresh at noon and swept into the corners at closing, where it waits for morning. ¶ Demos was seating a man who would rather have stood. He had hair parted dead center and flattened with something that smells of violets. Amato was jingling the change in his pocket like a meter running. Teitel was eating a baked potato out of his coat pocket. Mrs. Krantz was drinking lemon tea with the lemon left in. ¶ Mabry had said he was here at eight and nine. Mrs. Rafferty’s list had Amato at Rafferty’s at eight and nine. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “A gentleman orders the chop, sir. A man with something on his mind orders the soup. A man with something worse orders nothing and asks for the check.”
card: The room had the late quiet of a place that stays open because nobody ever told it to close.

before: I headed downtown and east for the Stannard flat, a fair few blocks away. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ I went back to the Stannard flat, because there’s no such thing as a place you’re finished with. ¶ Stannard, my client, had beaten me there and was waiting on the landing, with his coat on and his hands in his pockets. ¶ Before I asked anybody anything more, I wanted another look at where Caruso had been.
card: The place smelled of soap and supper and somebody’s good intentions.

before: A few blocks downtown and east, and I was at the Hirsch flat. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ The Hirsch flat again, a little later and a little quieter. ¶ Dr. Hirsch was there ahead of me, hat in her hands, turning the brim. ¶ Mimi had gone from here. I wanted another look before anybody tidied up.
card: It was warmer in than out, which was the best thing I could say for it. I said it.

before: The Peacock lay a fair few blocks uptown and west. The moon had moved along a few roofs since the last time I looked. It kept better hours than I did. ¶ Down in the cellar club it was the last set, for the serious drinkers, and the band had slowed to match them. Smoke hung under the low ceiling like a second ceiling. Through the velvet curtain at the foot of the stairs, four couples on the dance floor were holding each other up. There was the smell of lilies coming down through the floorboards from the undertaker’s, which the gin covers until about one. ¶ Mrs. Szabo was looking through the slot in the steel door. She had a nose that was broken once and set by somebody in a hurry, and a pair of pearl earrings to make up for it. Amato was jingling the change in his pocket like a meter running. Mrs. Blau was staring at a spot just over a stranger’s left shoulder. Glick was explaining to a man in perfect health what his funeral would cost. ¶ From her post Mrs. Szabo could see the street door through the slot, and the stairs down. “There’s one way in and one way out, and I’m sitting in both of them.”
card: The glasses behind the bar caught the light and did nothing else with it.

before: The Kit Kat was a few blocks uptown and west, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. I looked up for a lit window and found one. It wasn’t the same one, but it was doing the same job. ¶ Back at the Kit Kat. Nothing had moved but the clock. ¶ Stannard stood just inside the door with his back to the wall and his hands behind him. Whitfield had a table near the empty bandstand and was tapping the time of a song nobody was playing. Lanza sat at the back with her coat still on, as if she might leave at any minute and had been thinking so for an hour. Ellery was at the bar with his back to the room, watching the room in the mirror. ¶ Lanza had said she was here at nine and ten, and that Whitfield was with her at Feld’s studio at eight. That was reason enough.
card: The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

before: I walked it at an ordinary pace, uptown to Donnelly’s place, a couple of blocks, and wrote it down. An hour only holds so many walks like that, and the first light was coming up over the river, thin and gray. The streetlamps hadn’t heard about it yet. ¶ Back at Donnelly’s place, everything was where I’d left it except the time. ¶ Lathrop let me in and then stayed in the hall, the way people do when they don’t want to look at a room. ¶ Donnelly had died here. That was reason enough for the walk.
card: I wiped my feet, because somebody in that house would notice if I didn’t.

before: I set off uptown and west for the Peacock. It was a fair few blocks. My shoes had let the rain in two blocks back, and now they were just carrying it around for me. ¶ Down in the cellar club it was the last set, for the serious drinkers, and the band had slowed to match them. Smoke hung under the low ceiling like a second ceiling. Through the velvet curtain at the foot of the stairs, four couples on the dance floor were holding each other up. There was the slot in the steel door, the size of a letter box, through which the doorkeeper decides what kind of night you’re going to have. ¶ Mrs. Szabo was eating a pickle out of a paper bag on her stool. She had big hands folded in her lap, the knuckles flattened by a career she doesn’t discuss. Mrs. Krantz was counting bills with a rubber thumb. Teitel was eating a baked potato out of his coat pocket. ¶ From her post Mrs. Szabo could see the street door through the slot, and the stairs down. “Every face comes to my slot first. I don’t like most of them, so the ones I let in, I remember.”
card: I found a place at the bar and let the room settle around me.

before: The boxes at the Lyric was a fair few blocks uptown, and I took it at a good clip. Somewhere a radio was still arguing. It had been at it all night and hadn’t won yet. ¶ The boxes at the Lyric were four little balconies of gilt and red plush hung either side of the stage, each with six gold chairs and a curtain you could draw. From inside one you could see the whole stage and half the audience, and with the curtain drawn the audience couldn’t see you, which is what the boxes are mostly for. An old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more was nailed to the wall. ¶ Margolis was wiping his hands on a rag that made them dirtier. He had a cigar box under his arm that he never puts down, and never opens in company. ¶ He had found Russo. That was reason enough for the walk. Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had.
card: The room had been arranged so that nobody in it was ever quite facing anybody else.

before: Russo’s place was a few blocks downtown, near enough for anybody to walk it there and back inside the hour. I made a note of that. The first light was coming up over the river, thin and gray, and the streetlamps hadn’t heard about it yet. ¶ Russo’s place again. The welcome was about what it had been the first time. ¶ Dr. Hirsch, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ This was where Russo had died. Everything else would be somebody’s story, and the room wouldn’t.
card: A clock in the hall was keeping time for nobody in particular.

before: It was a few blocks to the Ostrow flat, east. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ The Ostrow flat looked the same the second time, which in my line of work is never quite true. ¶ My client, Mrs. Ostrow, had beaten me there and stood just inside the door, gloves in her hand. ¶ Mimi had gone from here. That was reason enough for the walk.
card: My feet were glad to stop, and said so.

before: Dr. Hirsch’s surgery was round the corner. Anybody could have made it there and back in an hour, and I wrote that down. The street was as empty as a street gets, which in this city is never quite empty. ¶ The dentist’s rooms over the bank were dark except the frosted door, which glowed a little from the streetlamp behind it. The waiting room had six chairs, a rubber plant and a table of magazines. The rubber plant looked the most patient. There was a cylinder of laughing gas on a trolley, with a rubber mask that has seen a great many faces at their worst. ¶ Miss Gutman was reading a movie magazine with her lips pressed shut. Teeth so perfect people assume the doctor did them; she was born with them, and she’ll tell you. ¶ Dr. Hirsch had said she was here at eight. That was reason enough. From her post Miss Gutman could see the waiting room and the stairs up from the street. “I may forget a name, but I write the name down. The face I keep.”
card: I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

before: I went round the corner to the flats over Lipsky’s. A man was selling chestnuts on the corner, and the fog stood round his brazier like customers who weren’t buying. ¶ Rain came down Orchard Street hard enough to bounce, and the pushcarts along the curb had their tarpaulins tied down over tomorrow’s stock like sheeted furniture in a shut house. The iron awning over the stoop of the flats over Lipsky’s dripped onto the third step exactly, so that everybody who went in after midnight went in with one wet shoulder. There were the iron shutters on the cloth shop, which come down at suppertime with a crash the whole street hears and go up in the morning with another. ¶ Miss Moskin was doing her stretching exercises on the landing, to the annoyance of the stairs. ¶ Nobody there was paid to keep track of anybody.
card: I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

before: The band room at the Peacock lay a couple of blocks east. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ The band room at the Peacock was a cupboard under the stairs with ideas above itself: an upright piano with three dead keys, a row of hooks with the band’s street coats on them, and a mirror with a bulb either side, one of them working. Every instrument case on the floor stood open. Like a mouth waiting to be fed. There was a velvet curtain at the foot of the stairs, once red, now the color of a bruise. ¶ Mabry was tapping out a tempo on the table with two fingers. He had a pencil mustache trimmed so thin it looks drawn on, and might have been. ¶ He had the room from the hour that mattered, and not before. Before that, he said, it was anybody’s.
card: The room had been arranged so that nobody in it was ever quite facing anybody else.
place: the band room at the Peacock

before: Dr. Hirsch’s flat lay a few blocks downtown. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ Behind its own front door the Excelsior was asleep: a good door, with a brass knob and a wooden wedge holding it open an inch for some tenant who keeps losing his key. The lobby mirror gave me back a man who needed a shave and a better coat. Nobody watches this door; that’s what the tenants pay for. There were marble stairs to the second floor and plain wood after that, where the builder ran out of marble or interest. ¶ Dr. Hirsch was reading a journal with her spectacles pushed up on her forehead, and she had steel-rimmed spectacles that she looks over, not through, when she doesn’t believe you. ¶ Mrs. Sobel had said Dr. Hirsch was with her at Mrs. Sobel’s place at ten, and that was worth the walk. Nobody kept a list of who came and went, on paper or in their head.
card: I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

before: A few blocks uptown, and I was at the flats over Lipsky’s. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ It was a clear night over Orchard Street, the kind that shows you every washing line strung between the buildings. The tenement over Lipsky’s had more than its share. A whole family’s shirts hung out over the street on a pulley, white as a surrender, waiting for a sun that wasn’t due till six. There was a row of tin mailboxes in the hall, with the names in five different hands and two crossed out. ¶ Miss Kahane, with a cane, was counting union dues into a cocoa tin. She had a red scarf, and a voice with a soapbox in it, even when she’s asking the time. Amato, in a sailor’s pea coat, was eating a sandwich at the kitchen window with one eye on his cab in the street. Mrs. Sobel, with a bandaged hand, was complaining to the janitor through the radiator. Miss Lowenthal was winding a metronome. ¶ Mrs. Krantz had said Miss Lowenthal borrowed Fritz most evenings. That settled where I was going. ¶ Nobody kept a list of who came and went, on paper or in their head.
card: I wiped my feet, because somebody in that house would notice if I didn’t.

before: Getting to the card room meant a couple of blocks uptown and east, and the dance hall crowd would have finished saying goodnight by now. It had taken them long enough, but they’d done it properly. ¶ The card room over the Bowery garage had no sign and no name on the door, only a light under it. A gambling room doesn’t advertise. The people who need it always find it. An old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more was nailed to the wall. ¶ Salerno had a chair in the corner and a cup of coffee, and the look of somebody who would say she was only passing. ¶ She had been at Petrosino’s at eight, for the fight party. That settled where I was going. ¶ No one was posted to see who came and went.
card: There was one light. Everybody had arranged to be just outside it.

before: I set off downtown for Steinmetz’s. It was a few blocks. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ The front of Steinmetz’s was dark, but the kitchen door at the back stood propped open on the alley, letting out steam and the sound of a pot being scrubbed by somebody with opinions about it. The chop house window still said CHOPS STEAKS OYSTERS in gold, with the R gone from OYSTERS. There was sawdust on the floor, fresh at noon and swept into the corners at closing, where it waits for morning. ¶ Demos was holding a fork up to the light. He had a white napkin over one forearm even off duty. He says he feels undressed without it. Miss Kahane was counting union dues into a cocoa tin. Mrs. Pomerantz was taking a pin out of her mouth to say something and putting it back instead. ¶ Teitel had said he was here at nine, with her. That settled where I was going. ¶ From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “A gentleman orders the chop, sir. A man with something on his mind orders the soup. A man with something worse orders nothing and asks for the check.”
card: I took it all in, which didn’t take long, and then took it in again.

before: Getting to the Lyric meant a fair few blocks uptown, and the cold was still out there doing its rounds. It’s the only thing in this city that works all night for nothing. ¶ The Lyric’s doors were chained for the night, and the cold had frosted the glass of the poster cases, so that THE RABBI’S DAUGHTER looked out at Second Avenue through a fog of her own. Inside, the boiler was knocking itself awake for the matinee, and a cleaning woman’s pail stood in the lobby with the mop in it at attention. There were pigeons in the ventilator over the gallery, who coo in the quiet parts. ¶ Pinsky was sweeping sunflower shells out of the gallery, and he had a white mustache waxed to points so fine they quiver when he disapproves. Mrs. Pomerantz was taking a pin out of her mouth to say something and putting it back instead. Belkin was telling a story about Odessa in 1899. ¶ Teitel had said he was here at eight, and that Mrs. Pomerantz was with him at Steinmetz’s at nine, and that was worth the walk. ¶ From his post Pinsky could see the whole house, from the back of the center aisle. “I seat by the chart. Every seat sold is a cross, every cross has a face, and I could draw you the face.”
card: I stood at the back a moment, where the people who work a theater always stand.

before: Kowalski’s lay a couple of blocks east. A policeman on his round tried a shop door, found it locked, and looked almost disappointed. ¶ I went to Mrs. Kowalski’s boarding house on Orchard Street. It was a narrow brick house with a scrubbed stoop and a smell of beet soup that had got into the walls and settled. The stair had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Kowalski was in the hall with a dustpan, sweeping a stair that had been swept already. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Havemeyer answered the door in her stocking feet, with the lamp behind her. Colquitt was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. ¶ Pickering had said she was here at nine, and that Havemeyer was with her at the Velvet Room at eight, and that was worth the walk. ¶ Nobody comes or goes in a rooming house without the landlady knowing, and Mrs. Kowalski had the look of a landlady who made a point of it.
card: I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

before: From there to Lindemann’s place was a few blocks, and the rain had the street to itself and was making the most of it. ¶ Lindemann’s place again, a little later and a little quieter. ¶ Hanrahan was there, with a cup of something she hadn’t touched and her coat still buttoned. ¶ Lindemann had died here. I wanted another look at the room before I asked anybody anything more.
card: I took it all in, which didn’t take long, and then took it in again.

before: It was a few blocks from there to Moskowitz’s, uptown and west, with my collar up. Second Avenue was running with water, curb to curb. ¶ I let myself back into Moskowitz’s. Nobody made a fuss about it. ¶ Ashby, in a camel coat, had a table by the window and a glass of tea gone cold. Callahan was still there.
card: I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

before: I set off uptown and west for the Orpheum. It was a couple of blocks. I thought of the couple under the umbrella. They’d have got somewhere by now, or given up and found a doorway. ¶ I went in at the Orpheum, a picture house with continuous shows till midnight. The last show had let out, the screen was a big gray blank, and the rows were full of peanut shells and dropped programs. A big brass ashtray full of sand stood by the inner doors, with a neat pattern raked into the sand. ¶ Bellucci was by the inner doors, sorting a stack of programs into the ones that could be used again and the ones that couldn’t. The uniform coat had the theater’s name on the collar, and the cap had been reshaped by a hundred hot nights. Lanza, in a green hat, sat in an aisle seat about halfway down, with her coat folded on her knees. ¶ Kreuzer had been here earlier in the evening. That was reason enough. An usher with a flashlight sees every face that comes in out of the street, and most of them twice.
card: I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

before: Sokol’s was a couple of blocks uptown and west, and I took it at a good clip. I heard footsteps behind me in the fog and stopped, and they stopped, and I stood there a while before I worked out they were mine. ¶ Sokol’s bakery window had a card in it, lettered by hand, RYE PUMPERNICKEL CHALLAH FRIDAYS, and behind the card the shop was dark except for the glow under the oven doors. Through the back, past the door marked FLOUR, you could hear the radio and the clink of somebody being poured a second one before he’d asked for it. There was a cigar box under the till for lottery slips, which the barman calls receipts. ¶ Sokol was slicing rye for a free lunch nobody eats. He had a row of old burns across the back of one hand, in stripes, from an oven rack that got him in 1911. Miss Nowak was saying ‘Number, please’ to nobody, out of habit. Miss Kahane was counting union dues into a cocoa tin. Mrs. Greco was telling her beads with flour still on her hands. ¶ From his post he could see the bar, the four tables and the door through from the bakery. “I count glasses. Every glass that goes out comes back, and I know whose hand it came back in.”
card: The glasses behind the bar caught the light and did nothing else with it.

before: I headed downtown and east for Moe’s, a few blocks away. The doorways along here were full of people waiting out the rain. Nobody offered to share. ¶ Moe’s again, a little later and a little quieter. ¶ Obermann was behind the bar with both hands spread on it, the way somebody stands who has been standing since the afternoon and has opinions about it. Lathrop was at the bar with a drink he wasn’t drinking. Thorndike was in a booth by the wall, alone with a glass of beer and a newspaper. Ainsworth sat at a little table by the wall, with a beer going flat in front of her. ¶ She had said Lathrop was with her here at ten. It was reason enough to look.
card: The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

before: I went round the corner to Sokol’s. A lit window hung in the fog above me with nothing holding it up. ¶ The bar behind Sokol’s bakery was shut, which there means the chairs were up and the barman was still at it, drying glasses and counting them onto a towel. In the front the ovens were coming back up for the morning. The whole place smelled of yeast and gin, which is the smell of a man with two jobs and no sleep. There was the door from the bakery to the bar, with FLOUR painted on it, which has fooled nobody for years. ¶ Sokol was humming a song from the old country into a glass while he dried it. He had eyes red at the rims from being up since four, every day, for nineteen years. Miss Nowak was saying ‘Number, please’ to nobody, out of habit. Russo was playing gin rummy against himself at a corner table, and cheating. Lieb was eating peanuts out of his hat. ¶ Russo had found Kaminsky. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. From his post Sokol could see the bar, the four tables and the door through from the bakery. “I don’t look up when the door goes. I look up when it doesn’t, because then somebody is standing in it deciding.”
card: I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

before: The Lyric was a few blocks west, and I took it at a good clip. The fog was still at the end of whatever street I was on. It followed me better than I follow people. ¶ The Lyric had let out, and Second Avenue in front of it had the look of a party after the guests have gone: programs in the gutter, a hat on a hydrant, and the café across the street full of actors explaining the play to each other. In the lobby the lights were down to one chandelier, and the brass rail round the box office was still warm from hands. There were sunflower-seed shells in the gallery aisles, swept up every night and back by the second act. ¶ Pinsky was pointing his flashlight at a man who was talking. He had a white mustache waxed to points so fine they quiver when he disapproves. Russo was sitting with his back to the wall. Mrs. Blau was staring at a spot just over a stranger’s left shoulder. Teitel was eating a baked potato out of his coat pocket. ¶ Mrs. Blau had been at Dr. Hirsch’s at eight, for the card party. It was reason enough to look. ¶ From his post Pinsky could see the whole house, from the back of the center aisle. “From the back of the aisle I see the back of every head in the place, and the back of a head tells you more than a face: who leans, who doesn’t laugh, who keeps turning round to look at the doors.”
card: I stood at the back a moment, where the people who work a theater always stand.

before: Moskowitz’s lay a couple of blocks west. Second Avenue was running with water, curb to curb. ¶ I let myself back into Moskowitz’s, and nobody made a fuss about it. ¶ Brennan, the head waiter, was standing by the coats with a menu under his arm, in case anybody wanted one at this hour. Rafferty, Hanrahan and Reinhardt were still there.
card: I stood a moment and let my eyes catch up with the rest of me.

before: The Russo flat was a fair few blocks downtown and east, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. I looked up for a lit window and found one. It wasn’t the same one, but it was doing the same job. ¶ Back at the Russo flat. Nothing had moved but the clock. ¶ Russo was there ahead of me, hat in his hands, turning the brim. ¶ Fritz had gone from here. I wanted another look before anybody tidied up.
card: I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

before: The Callahan flat was a long walk uptown and west, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. The fog was going gray at the top, which was how I knew the morning had started without me. ¶ Back at the Callahan flat. Nothing had moved but the clock. ¶ Callahan, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ Before I asked anybody anything more, I wanted another look at where Fritz had been.
card: Nobody offered to take my hat. I hadn’t expected anybody to.

before: From there to the Blue Lantern was a couple of blocks. My shoes had let the rain in two blocks back, and now they were just carrying it around for me. ¶ I went to the Blue Lantern, a cellar club behind a laundry, through the steam of the laundry and down a flight of stone steps. The band had packed up for the night, and the talk had got quieter and closer, the way talk does in a cellar after midnight. A glass globe hung from the ceiling with half its little mirrors gone, turning slowly over the dance floor. ¶ Moretti was on a chair tipped back against the door frame, chewing a toothpick down to splinters. Heavy in the coat and light on his feet, he had the door swung wide before I’d reached for it, and shut again before I’d decided anything. Donnelly, in a camel coat, had a table near the empty bandstand and was tapping the time of a song nobody was playing. ¶ Ainsworth had been here earlier in the evening. It was reason enough to look. Nobody gets into a place like this without Moretti looking them over first, and he looks people over for a living.
card: I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

before: The Kit Kat was a few blocks west, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. The street was as empty as a street gets, which in this city is never quite empty. ¶ I went up the outside stair to the Kit Kat, a speakeasy over a garage. The garage underneath was shut for the night, but the room still smelled of motor oil under the perfume and the cigarettes. There was a coat-check window by the door with a bell on the counter and a sign that said Not Responsible. ¶ Obermann was on a stool by the door with a newspaper she wasn’t reading. Heavy in the coat and light on her feet, she had the door swung wide before I’d reached for it, and shut again before I’d decided anything. Marchetti had a table near the empty bandstand and was tapping the time of a song nobody was playing. ¶ Obermann opens the door to everybody who comes in and shuts it behind everybody who goes, which means she sees the evening from about two feet away.
card: The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

before: Glick’s place was only round the corner, which I wrote down: the whole night was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. Ludlow Street was running with water, curb to curb. ¶ Back at Glick’s place. Nothing had moved but the clock. ¶ Miss Kahane was there, with a cup of something she hadn’t touched and her coat still buttoned. ¶ Glick had died here. I wanted another look at the room before I asked anybody anything more.

before: The Kit Kat was a few blocks west, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. When a truck backed in downstairs, every glass in the room went up half an inch and came down again, and nothing spilled. They’d had practice. A row of paper lanterns was strung across the room, faded from red to pink by years of smoke. ¶ Kavanagh was on a stool by the door with a newspaper she wasn’t reading. Tillman was at the bar with her back to the room, watching the room in the mirror. Feeney had a table near the empty bandstand and was tapping the time of a song nobody was playing. ¶ Kavanagh opens the door to everybody who comes in and shuts it behind everybody who goes, which means she sees the evening from about two feet away.

before: The Automat was a couple of blocks uptown and west, and I took it at a good clip. before: A good walk uptown and west, and I was at Wexler’s. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ The front of Steinmetz’s was dark, but the kitchen door at the back stood propped open on the alley, letting out steam and the sound of a pot being scrubbed by somebody with opinions about it. The chop house window still said CHOPS STEAKS OYSTERS in gold, with the R gone from OYSTERS. There was an umbrella stand made from an elephant’s foot. Which the owner swears is a cow’s. ¶ Demos was writing covers in the book at his stand. He had a white napkin over one forearm even off duty. He says he feels undressed without it. Miss Kahane was counting union dues into a cocoa tin. Glick was explaining to a man in perfect health what his funeral would cost. Miss Moskin was reading Variety for parts uptown.

before: The Shamrock was a fair few blocks downtown and east, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. The streetlamps went out all at once while I was under one, which felt personal. ¶ The Shamrock, a bar on the corner, had its windows painted green up to the height of a hat, so that Avenue B could see the lights were on and nothing else. Inside it smelled of beer and a radiator working harder than it was paid to. There was a radio on a shelf behind the bar, playing dance music so softly it might have been coming from next door. ¶ Brauer was behind the bar, setting clean glasses upside down in rows on a towel. She had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Tramonti was at the bar with a drink he wasn’t drinking.
lead: Mosley had said Tramonti was with her at her place at nine.
card: Mosley had said he was with her at her place at nine. That settled where I was going.

before: A good walk west, and I was at the Blue Lantern. The rain had the street to itself and was making the most of it. ¶ The Blue Lantern, a cellar club behind a laundry, smelled faintly of starch, which is more than any other club in the city can say. The lantern over the bandstand was blue, as promised, and so was most of the music. A row of paper lanterns was strung across the room, faded from red to pink by years of smoke. ¶ Vitale was on a chair tipped back against the door frame, chewing a toothpick down to splinters. Heavy in the coat and light on her feet, she had the door swung wide before I’d reached for it, and shut again before I’d decided anything. Pickering was at the bar with her back to the room, watching the room in the mirror. Mosley sat at the back with her coat still on, as if she might leave at any minute and had been thinking so for an hour.

Russo sat at the end of the long bench by the wall, with a glass of ginger ale and a very straight back. Lieb was practicing a fox-trot step in a corner by himself.
lead: Mrs. Ostrow had sat here telling the room about her key.

before: It was a fair few blocks to the Peacock, uptown and west. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ Down in the cellar club it was the last set, for the serious drinkers, and the band had slowed to match them. Smoke hung under the low ceiling like a second ceiling. Through the velvet curtain at the foot of the stairs, four couples on the dance floor were holding each other up. There was the slot in the steel door, the size of a letter box, through which the doorkeeper decides what kind of night you’re going to have. ¶ Mrs. Szabo was explaining to a large man why he was going home. She had a nose that was broken once and set by somebody in a hurry, and a pair of pearl earrings to make up for it. Dr. Hirsch was reading a journal with her spectacles pushed up on her forehead. Glick was explaining to a man in perfect health what his funeral would cost.

before: I set off downtown and east for the surgery at Dr. Hirsch’s surgery. It was a couple of blocks. A lamp on a jointed arm hung over the chair, and the window looked out on a brick wall six feet away, so the patients have nothing to look at but the doctor. An old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more was nailed to the wall. ¶ Doyle was writing a name in a little black book. Every pharmacy has that sign. Every pharmacist hopes you won’t. A supply company’s calendar hung behind the counter, with every day crossed off in pencil. ¶ Lefkowitz was behind her counter in a gray coat, doing the day’s figures by the light of one lamp. Neat and gray and precise, she wrote everything down, and I had the feeling I’d be written down too before long.

It was a narrow brick house with a scrubbed stoop and a smell of beet soup that had got into the walls and settled. The stair had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Kowalski was in the hall with a dustpan, sweeping a stair that had been swept already. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Tillman, in a green hat, was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into her collar. Hanrahan, in a camel coat, was at the window with the curtain held back an inch, keeping an eye on the street. Mulcahy, with a cane, answered the door in her stocking feet, with the lamp behind her.

before: Midnight. The office was where I’d left it, at the top of four flights on Mulberry Street, which is the only thing about it you could count on. The fee sat on the blotter where I’d dropped it, more money than the desk usually saw in a month. I left the lamp burning longer than I needed, so the two of them could get acquainted. ¶ Somebody knocked twice, politely, and then a third time, less politely. My visitor came in unhurried. As if the hour happened to other people. ¶ “Mimi’s gone,” Petrosino said. “My Persian. She sleeps on the window seat, and she isn’t there.” ¶ I offered him the chair and turned the lamp away from him. ¶ “I had people in at eight for cards,” he said. “Ellery, Thorndike and Doyle. Nobody else.” ¶ “I went out after them,” he said, “and I left the key under the mat for my sister. I told the table I would.” ¶ “When did this happen, as near as you can say?” ¶ “And I know when,” he said. “St. Teresa’s was striking ten when the woman across the hall heard the door.” ¶ “Who’d want to take her?” ¶ “If you want a name, it’s Thorndike,” he said. “She and I haven’t spoken since the business over the coal bill.” ¶ There was more, and he didn’t much want to say it. “Ellery, a cab driver, lost her job on Friday, and asked me what Mimi was worth. And Mimi bit Doyle, a milliner, at Easter, and he swore he’d see the back of her.” ¶ Ten dollars came out of a pocket that had been saving it for something better. “Find out who. And get Mimi back.”
card: I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

before: Midnight, and the office on Mulberry Street was as quiet as an office gets when nobody is paying for it to be loud. Rent was three weeks gone. The envelope wasn’t going to pay itself by sitting on the desk. I lit a cigarette off the lamp and let the smoke do the worrying. ¶ A shape came up against the frosted glass of the door, and then a knock that didn’t want to be a knock. My visitor came in unhurried, as if the hour happened to other people. ¶ “It’s Fritz,” Kavanagh said. “My dachshund. He’s gone from his basket by the stove.” ¶ I offered him the chair. He looked at it the way you’d look at a dog that might bite, and sat anyway. ¶ “I had people in at eight,” he said, “for cards. Crowninshield, Hochstetter and Mosley. Nobody else came.” ¶ “The lock has been broken since Tuesday,” he said. “I showed the whole table the locksmith’s card.” ¶ “When did this happen, as near as you can say?” ¶ He had it written on the back of an envelope, and read it out to me. “The family across the hall heard the door during the Atwater Kent Hour or the hour after it: nine or ten o’clock.” ¶ “Mrs. Brauer minds Fritz when I’m out,” he said. “She has rooms at Rafferty’s.” ¶ “Who’d want to take him?” ¶ “You might ask about Hochstetter,” he said. “She has wanted Fritz since the day I brought him home. That’s from the woman downstairs, and she hears most things.” ¶ There was more, and he didn’t much want to say it. “Fritz bit Mosley, a sewing-machine operator, at Easter, and she swore she’d see the back of him. And Hurwitz, a switchboard operator, and I haven’t spoken since the business over the coal bill.” ¶ He went round the room the way people do when they’ve had all night to think about it. “Crowninshield, a cab driver, is three weeks behind on the rent, and has been heard to say what a dachshund with papers fetches.” ¶ Ten dollars came out of a pocket that had been saving it for something better. “Find out who. And get Fritz back.”
card: I took the money and my hat, in that order.

before: Midnight. My office was a room over a tailor’s on Mulberry Street, with my name on the door in gold leaf that was coming off one letter at a time. My jaw had gone from purple to a color nobody sells paint in. Even the low lamp showed that much. The mirror could wait for morning. ¶ There was a knock, and then the door opened before I’d said anything, which is how people knock when they’ve made up their minds. My visitor set an engraved card on the desk before she said a word. I felt underdressed. ¶ She didn’t wait to be asked. “Angelina Ruggiero. Chandler Ainsworth’s sister, or I was till tonight, and nobody is doing anything about it.” ¶ Ainsworth was a bail bondsman. Donnelly, who’d come round to collect a debt, found the body in his own two rooms over the bakery on Hester Street at half past eleven. The police called it his heart and went home. ¶ I offered Ruggiero the chair. She looked at it the way you’d look at a dog that might bite, and sat anyway. ¶ “When did it happen?” ¶ She said it slowly, so that I’d get it right. “His mantel clock was knocked over and stopped at five past, but it was never right: nine or ten o’clock, I’d say.” ¶ “Every night it was the Blue Lantern, earlier on,” she said. “Tonight too. The usual.” ¶ “Who’d have wanted that?” ¶ “I found a letter from Zeldin in the desk,” she said. “He threw her out of a lease. Start there.” ¶ She put fifty dollars on the desk. “Find out who. The police aren’t going to.”
card: I folded the money into my pocket and reached for my hat.

before: Midnight. My office on Mulberry Street had my name on the door, a bottle in the drawer and the landlady’s bill under the bottle, where I could keep an eye on it. My head kept its own time, behind the clock over the safe and louder. I put the lamp low and thanked it. ¶ A shape came up against the frosted glass of the door, and then a knock that didn’t want to be a knock. My visitor came in with an apology for the hour and a second one for the first, and was well into a third before sitting down. ¶ “Somebody has taken my Pomeranian,” Brennan said. “Duchess. Gone from her cushion by the radiator, just like that.” ¶ “I had people in at eight for a christening supper,” he said. “Stannard, Lanza and Sweeney. Nobody else.” ¶ “The lock has been broken since Tuesday,” he said. “I showed the whole table the locksmith’s card.” ¶ “When did you last see her?” ¶ “I can tell you when, near enough,” he said. “The boy from the delicatessen came up with an order at a quarter past ten and passed somebody on the dark stairs, going down in a hurry.” ¶ “Who’d have a reason?” ¶ “Look at Sweeney,” he said. “He asked twice whether Duchess had papers at the christening supper. Who does that? And he and I haven’t spoken since the business over the coal bill.” ¶ There was more, and he didn’t much want to say it. “Lanza, a bookmaker, has wanted Duchess since the day I brought her home. And Stannard, a switchboard operator, owes Lou the bookmaker forty dollars, and Lou takes things in kind.” ¶ “Ten dollars,” he said. “It’s what I have. Find out who, and where.”
card: I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

before: Midnight. I was in my office on Mulberry Street, going over the month’s bills by the desk lamp. Rent was three weeks gone. The envelope wasn’t going to pay itself by sitting on the desk. Water ran down the gutters in a hurry, carrying a newspaper with it. ¶ Ludlow Street after midnight smelled of dill and coal smoke, and the dill was coming from the Belvedere, where the pickle barrels stood along the shop front under chained-down lids, getting on with it in the dark. Above them the flats went up five floors, a light here and there, and somewhere a radio was playing a song about the moon to somebody trying to sleep. There were five flights of stairs worn into a dip in the middle of every tread, with a gas jet turned low on each landing. ¶ Glick was in the chair by the table, head down on folded arms, like somebody asleep over the accounts. He had his collection book in his breast pocket, paid up to Friday, and a pencil behind each ear. ¶ Miss Kahane let me in and then stayed in the hall, the way people do when they don’t want to look at a room. ¶ There was no one to notice who passed through. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and whoever did it had walked in here with the rat poison already in hand.
card: I took my hat off. It seemed like the thing to do.

before: From there to Dandridge’s place was a few blocks. The fog had got in among the late crowd, and people stepped from the fog laughing and went back into it the same way. ¶ I went up to Dandridge’s flat on the top floor of 12 Ludlow Street. By the top floor I had a stitch in my side and an opinion about stairs, and the opinion was not kind. An empty birdcage hung in the corner, with nothing in it but a little swing. ¶ Dandridge lay by the door, face down. Nobody had moved the body, and nobody had wanted to. ¶ Reinhardt had got there before me and looked up when I came in, the way people look up when they’re paying for your time. ¶ Nobody kept a list of who came and went, on paper or in their head. ¶ If it happened at ten, it happened in this room, and Dandridge had let whoever did it in.
card: I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

before: I set off east for the Shapiro flat. It was a couple of blocks. The rain had driven everybody into the doorways, where they stood smoking and watching it like a show nobody had paid for. ¶ The Shapiro flat over the delicatessen on Second Avenue was three small rooms kept very clean, with oilcloth on the kitchen table and a calendar from the delicatessen on the wall. A china shepherdess stood on a doily, looking at the room with painted patience. ¶ Shapiro showed me where the spoons had been kept and touched the place once, lightly, the way you touch a sore tooth. ¶ Nobody kept a list of who came and went, on paper or in their head. ¶ If it went at ten, the flat had been empty, and anybody who’d heard Shapiro at the Blue Lantern had known the way in. That was a room, more or less. It was a big room.
card: I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

before: The Doyle flat was a good walk uptown and east, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. A dance hall upstairs was letting out, and the street was full of people saying goodnight at length. ¶ The Doyle parlor floor on Stuyvesant Street was two tall rooms with folding doors between them, a thick carpet and a smell of beeswax. There was an upright piano against the wall with a lace runner on top and photographs standing along it like a family on a station platform. ¶ Doyle had left everything just as it was, so that Mimi would know the way home. ¶ Nobody there was paid to keep track of anybody. ¶ If she went at nine or ten, she went after the christening supper, and everybody at the christening supper had known the way in.
card: I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

before: Wojcik’s list had Miss Lowenthal here all evening, so that was where I went next. The janitor knocks his pipe out on the stoop rail so often the rail has a dent in it the shape of the bowl. She had long fingers that tap out scales on whatever’s in front of them: a table, a banister, your sleeve. ¶ I asked her to tell me her evening, from the beginning, and not to leave out the dull parts. ¶ She went slowly, the way people do who like to get things right. ¶ “My evening was quiet, and I could be quiet about it, but since you ask, here it is. I was home at the flats over Lipsky’s all evening. Miss Moskin was there at eight; Belkin was there at nine; Miss Moskin was there at ten.” ¶ So here at ten and eight, with Miss Moskin, which was what Wojcik had.
card: That much of it stood up, and it stood up where I could check it.

before: Sirkin’s list had Zeldin here at ten. I wanted the rest of it in Zeldin’s own words. I sat one seat over. ¶ I asked her where she’d been tonight, and who with, hour by hour. ¶ She gave it to me in as few words as the evening would go into. ¶ “I was at the Shamrock from eight through nine. Reinhardt was there at eight; at nine it was just me. Come ten, I went to the Thalia, because a friend was in the show, with Bellucci.” ¶ So here at ten, with Bellucci, which was what Sirkin had.
card: At an hour that mattered, somebody else could vouch for it.

before: Teitel had said Glick was with him here at ten, so I went over. I kept my voice down. Glick kept his eyes on me. He had a little leather book of weekly payments in his breast pocket, and the habit of patting it, the way other men pat for a wallet. ¶ I asked him where he’d been tonight. All of it, in order. ¶ He took a moment to put the evening in order before he handed it over. ¶ “My evening, in full. I believe in being fully covered. I was at Steinmetz’s all evening. At eight it was just me; Teitel was there at nine and ten. Ten, I take my pulse. It’s been fine for forty-four years, but you can’t be too careful.” ¶ So here at ten, with Teitel, and at eight, which was what Demos had.
card: At an hour that mattered, somebody else could vouch for it.

before: I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Miss Nowak. The barman counts the glasses onto a towel at closing, and when one is short he knows whose it was. She had nails painted red and bitten, both. ¶ “Where were you tonight?” I said. “All of it. I’ve got time, and I hope you have.” She counted back through the evening under her breath before saying any of it out loud. ¶ “I don’t mind telling you. I’m very good at times; it’s my whole job. I was at Russo’s at eight, for the christening supper, with Dr. Hirsch and Mrs. Greco. Around nine I left the christening supper early and went home to change, and stayed through ten. Miss Kahane and Mrs. Greco were there at nine; at ten it was just me. At eleven I went to Sokol’s to see who was in, with Miss Kahane and Mrs. Greco.” ¶ So the Russo flat at eight, with Dr. Hirsch and Mrs. Greco, which was what Russo had said.
after: For ten, the hour that mattered, Miss Nowak said home at Rafferty’s.
card: That part of the evening, at least, somebody else could vouch for.

before: I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Lanza. I said who I was, and she took it about as well as people do. She was neat in a way that took effort: every button done, the collar pinned, the hair flat. The hands stayed folded until she needed one, and then only the one. ¶ “Tell me where you were tonight,” I said. “Every hour, and anybody who can say so.” She thought for a second, the way anybody does, and started at the beginning. ¶ “I was at Mosley’s at eight, for the card party, with Carbone. At nine I left the card party early and had a ticket for the Orpheum, with Coffin. Ten o’clock I stopped in at the Velvet Room to get warm, on my own.” ¶ So the Mosley flat at eight, with Carbone, which was what Mosley had said.
after: For ten, the hour that mattered, Lanza said the Velvet Room.
card: That part of the evening, at least, somebody else could vouch for.

before: I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Miss Nowak. She was saying ‘Number, please’ to nobody, out of habit. She was pale under a cloche hat, with a red mark across the top of her head from the headset that her hair doesn’t quite hide. ¶ I asked her for her evening, in order, the way you’d ask for a receipt. She smoothed the front of her coat, as if the evening were on it, and began. ¶ “I don’t mind telling you. I’m very good at times; it’s my whole job. I was at Mrs. Krantz’s at eight, for the supper, with Amato and Russo. Come nine, I left the supper to get some air and went to the Lyric, because a friend was in the show, with Belkin. Around ten I went to Steinmetz’s for coffee and pie, on my own.” ¶ So the Krantz flat at eight, with Amato and Russo, which was what Mrs. Krantz had said.
after: Miss Nowak said Steinmetz’s for ten, the hour that mattered.
card: That part of the evening, at least, somebody else could vouch for.

before: I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Cheatham. ¶ I took out my pencil, which makes some people nervous and makes the rest feel important. “Where were you tonight?” I said. “All of it. I’ve got time, and I hope you have.” ¶ He told it the way you give somebody directions, landmark by landmark. ¶ “I was at Petrosino’s at eight, for the card party, with Sirkin. At nine I left the card party when the cards went badly and went to the second show at the Thalia, with Dandridge. Ten o’clock I went to the chop house to read the late paper over a plate of soup, by myself.” ¶ The Petrosino flat at eight, with Sirkin, which was what Petrosino had said.
after: For ten, the hour that mattered, Cheatham said the chop house.
card: So far as it went, it stood up.

before: Glick was polishing his derby with his sleeve. He had a black derby a size too small, which he raises an inch to everybody, like a man lifting the lid on a pot. ¶ “Tell me where you were tonight,” I said. “Every hour, and anybody who can say so.” He asked why I wanted to know, and then told me before I could answer. ¶ “My evening, in full. I believe in being fully covered. At eight I went round to the flats over Lipsky’s to borrow a collar stud, with Miss Lowenthal. At nine I went to the Peacock, because a friend was on the door, with Miss Kahane and Mrs. Blau. Ten o’clock I dropped a parcel off at the flats over Lipsky’s, with Mrs. Blau and Miss Lowenthal. Ten, I take my pulse. It’s been fine for forty-four years, but you can’t be too careful. Then at eleven I went to the Peacock to see who was about, on my own.” ¶ The flats over Lipsky’s at eight and at ten, with Mrs. Blau, which was what Miss Lowenthal had said.
after: He said the Peacock for eleven, the hour that mattered.
card: So far as it went, it stood up.

before: Sokol’s list had Mrs. Pomerantz here at eight, nine and eleven, so I went over. I took the stool next to her. She had a velvet pincushion strapped to her wrist like a watch, bristling. ¶ I asked her where she’d been tonight, and who with, hour by hour. ¶ She kept it short. before: Miss Kahane was counting union dues into a cocoa tin. ¶ “Sokol has you at Sokol’s at eight. Now tell me the rest of it, from the beginning.” ¶ She said she would tell me once, and I’d better be listening. ¶ “Where was I. I’ll tell you, and I’ll tell you straight, which is more than the police ever got out of a boss. At seven I dropped a parcel off at Rafferty’s, with Mrs. Blau. Then at eight I wanted company, so I went to Sokol’s, and stayed through nine. Come ten, I went down to the stock room at the Peacock for a quiet drink out of the way. Ten, I count the dues. Four dollars and sixty cents. The revolution’s been put off again. I had nobody with me at eight, nine or ten.” ¶ She said Sokol’s at nine, but Sokol had Miss Moskin and Mrs. Blau at Sokol’s at nine o’clock, and nobody else. ¶ The tin sign on the wall had outlasted the company and would outlast me. ¶ The Turn: Somebody Wasn’t There ¶ I found a doorway and stood in it, and let the whole night go past me again, in order. ¶ Here’s what I had. place: the stock room at the Peacock

before: I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Miss Lowenthal. ¶ She was marking a sheet of music with tiny furious pencil notes. She had long fingers that tap out scales on whatever’s in front of them: a table, a banister, your sleeve. “Wojcik has you here at eight. Now tell me the rest of it, from the beginning.” ¶ She took a moment to put the evening in order before she handed it over. ¶ “Certainly. I shall be brief and in tempo. I was at Sokol’s at seven, with Doyle and Dr. Hirsch. Come eight, I went home to change, with Dr. Hirsch. Around nine I went down to the stock room at the Peacock for a quiet drink out of the way. Nine is for music I play for myself. Slow music. Nobody needs to hear it. At ten I turned in early, home at the flats over Lipsky’s. I had nobody with me at nine or ten.” ¶ She said home at ten, but Wojcik had nobody here at ten o’clock. ¶ Correcting an exercise book in red pencil: that was the last I saw of her. ¶ The Turn: A Hole in the Evening ¶ I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest. ¶ Here’s what I had. It happened at nine or ten o’clock, and I didn’t know which yet. Dr. Hirsch was at the flats over Lipsky’s at nine. Wojcik said so. Miss Lowenthal had told me home at ten, and Wojcik’s list said otherwise. Doyle and Kaminsky hadn’t told me where they were at nine or ten. Nobody else had either. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to go over the table.
card: That was everything I had. It wasn’t enough yet.

before: Dr. Hirsch had said she was here at eight and ten, and Sokol had been here to see who came and went. ¶ The barman counts the glasses onto a towel at closing, and when one is short he knows whose it was. I asked Sokol who’d been here tonight, and said I’d take it untidy, the way it happened. ¶ He answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice. ¶ “Seven, I take the last tray out and unlock the door that says flour. One job stops, the other one starts. Seven o’clock, Doyle, Amato, Kaminsky and Russo, and nobody else that hour. Eight, Doyle and Dr. Hirsch, and nobody else. Nine, Doyle and Russo, and nobody else at all. Ten, Doyle and Kaminsky. Nobody else. If there was, there’s a glass I can’t account for, and there isn’t.” ¶ Dr. Hirsch said Sokol’s at ten, but he had Doyle and Kaminsky here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. Doyle hadn’t been at the flats over Lipsky’s while it was there to take. Mrs. Greco had said nine or ten. Russo was at Sokol’s at nine, alive. ¶ Rubbing the barman’s eyes with the heels of both hands, like a man trying to put them back: that was the last I saw of him. ¶ The Turn: A Hole in the Evening ¶ I went over it once more, the way you go over a bill you know is wrong. ¶ Here’s what I had. Mrs. Greco had said nine or ten, and Russo was at Sokol’s at nine, alive. The rat poison came from the flats over Lipsky’s, so whoever used it had been there first. Doyle hadn’t. Doyle was at Sokol’s at nine and ten; Sokol said so. Kaminsky was at Sokol’s at ten. Sokol said so. Dr. Hirsch had told me Sokol’s at ten, and Sokol’s list said otherwise. Amato hadn’t told me where he was at nine or ten, and nobody else had either. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out from the janitor at the flats over Lipsky’s who’d been in.

before: Teitel had said Miss Lowenthal was with him at his place at eight, so I went over. I kept my voice down. She kept her eyes on me. She had long fingers that tap out scales on whatever’s in front of them: a table, a banister, your sleeve. ¶ I asked her where she’d been tonight, and who with, hour by hour. ¶ She looked at me for a while first, as if deciding what sort of question it was. ¶ “My evening was quiet, and I could be quiet about it, but since you ask, here it is. I was home at the flats over Lipsky’s all evening. Miss Kahane, Amato and Teitel were there at eight; Miss Kahane, Kaminsky and Amato were there at nine; Miss Kahane and Amato were there at ten; Amato and Mrs. Krantz were there at eleven. Eight, I make tea. A proper cup, with a saucer, whatever else is happening. I had Mimi at my place at ten, to keep the mice down, and put her back in the flat just before eleven.” ¶ For ten and eleven, the hours that mattered, she said home, here at the flats over Lipsky’s. It went in the notebook in her own words. ¶ Correcting an exercise book in red pencil: that was the last I saw of her. ¶ The Turn: The Story Comes Apart ¶ I stopped where I was and went over it again, slowly, the way you reread a letter from the bank. ¶ Here’s what I had. Doyle had said ten or eleven o’clock. I had evenings from Amato, Mrs. Krantz, Teitel and Miss Lowenthal, and I didn’t have Miss Kahane’s or Kaminsky’s evenings yet.
card: Some of it would hold and some of it wouldn’t. I didn’t know yet which was which.

before: Teitel had been watching me ask the others, and had had time to think about it, which isn’t always an advantage. He was folding a necktie into a pocket square for a man who hadn’t asked. He had a necktie of his own so loud it seems to be shouting for the others. ¶ “Mrs. Rafferty has you at Rafferty’s at eight and nine. I’d like the rest of your evening to go with it.” ¶ He answered straight off, the way people do with an evening they’ve only just finished. ¶ “For you, a special price: the whole evening, free. Nobody gets that from Teitel. Listen. At eight I went up to Rafferty’s to pay a call, and stayed through nine, with Mabry and Miss Nowak. Nine, business. I think about it; it doesn’t think about me. Ten o’clock I went to Steinmetz’s to read the late paper over a plate of soup, by myself.” ¶ He said Steinmetz’s at ten, but Demos had Mrs. Krantz and Miss Kahane here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. before: Lathrop’s list had Reinhardt here at eight. I wanted the rest of it in her own words. I sat down across from her. She moved her cup an inch closer, as though I might take it. ¶ “Tell me where you were tonight,” I said. “Every hour, and anybody who can say so.” She answered without looking at me, which is a way of answering. ¶ “I was at the Odessa at eight, with Margolis. Nine o’clock I took a letter round to the Delmonico rooms, with Hanrahan and Mrs. Thorndike. Then at ten I went in to the print shop to set type for the morning. Then I closed up at eleven and went to the Odessa for the blue-plate supper. At ten and eleven I was on my own.” ¶ She said the Odessa at eleven, but Lathrop had Hanrahan, Margolis and Lou here at eleven o’clock, and nobody else. ¶ One of those folded hands came unfolded, did something small, and went back. I’ve seen banks spend less carefully. ¶ The Turn: Not Where They Said ¶ I stopped where I was and went over it again, slowly, the way you reread a letter from the bank. ¶ Here’s what I had. Pickering had said ten or eleven, and at ten Fritz was at the Delmonico rooms. Reinhardt, Brennan and Margolis were at the Odessa while Pickering told the room. Hanrahan wasn’t. Reinhardt had told me the Odessa at eleven, and Lathrop’s list said otherwise. Hanrahan was at the Delmonico rooms at ten and the Odessa at eleven. Mrs. Thorndike and Lathrop said so. Margolis was at the Odessa at ten and eleven; Lathrop said so. Brennan hadn’t told me where she was at ten or eleven. Nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Lou at the Odessa at twelve.
card: That was everything I had. It wasn’t enough yet.

before: Obermann’s list had Mosley here at eight. I wanted to hear the other side of it. ¶ I didn’t waste his time. He looked like somebody who kept count of it. He smelled of gasoline and cold coffee and kept his gloves on indoors, the fingertips cut out of them. “Tell me where you were tonight,” I said. “Every hour, and anybody who can say so.” ¶ He kept it short. Some people do with everybody. ¶ “I was at the Orpheum at eight, with Abramowitz. Come nine, I went to the Palace to sit through the double bill. Around ten I went to the second show at the Orpheum. At eleven I looked in at the Palace again. At nine, ten and eleven I was on my own.” ¶ He said the Orpheum at ten, but Obermann had Abramowitz, Lathrop and Pardo here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. ¶ I could have used gloves like that. Mine have all ten fingertips, and they still let the cold in. ¶ The Turn: Two Stories ¶ I stopped where I was and went over it again, slowly, the way you reread a letter from the bank. ¶ Here’s what I had. Stannard had said nine or ten, and at nine Mimi was at Kowalski’s. Abramowitz, Rosenbaum and Mosley were at the Orpheum while Stannard told the room. Lathrop wasn’t. Abramowitz was at the Orpheum at nine and ten; Obermann said so. Lathrop was at Kowalski’s at nine and the Orpheum at ten. Mrs. Tillman and Obermann said so. Rosenbaum was at the Orpheum at nine; Obermann said so. Mosley had told me the Orpheum at ten, and Obermann’s list said otherwise. And whatever it was had gone to Pardo at the Orpheum at eleven. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to know what Rosenbaum had passed on the way to the Orpheum at nine.
card: Some of it would hold and some of it wouldn’t. I didn’t know yet which was which.

before: Sokol’s list had Dr. Hirsch here at nine. That was reason enough to ask. ¶ She was drinking a brandy at the bar with a medical journal propped on the bottles. She had steel-rimmed spectacles that she looks over, not through, when she doesn’t believe you. “Tell me where you were tonight,” I said. “Every hour, and anybody who can say so.” ¶ She went slowly, the way people do who like to get things right. ¶ “I keep good records. You’ll find my evening as precise as a filling, and about as much fun. I was at Kaminsky’s at eight, for the meeting, with Belkin and Miss Kahane. Eight, I start to want a cigarette, and I make myself wait till nine. Discipline. Around nine I left the meeting early and went to Sokol’s, as most nights, with Lieb. At ten I went up to the card room over Feingold’s garage to watch the game and not play. Eleven o’clock I went to Sokol’s to hear the fight on the radio. At ten and eleven I was on my own.” ¶ She said Sokol’s at eleven, but Sokol had Lieb, Miss Kahane and Fishel here at eleven o’clock, and nobody else. The rest of Dr. Hirsch’s evening held where I could check it: Kaminsky had her at the Kaminsky flat at eight, with Belkin. ¶ Smoking one cigarette very slowly at a window: that was the last I saw of her. ¶ The Turn: A Hole in the Evening ¶ I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest. ¶ Here’s what I had. Kaminsky had said ten or eleven, and at ten Caruso was at the flats over Lipsky’s. Dr. Hirsch, Belkin and Miss Kahane were at the meeting and knew the way in. Lieb wasn’t. Dr. Hirsch had told me Sokol’s at eleven, and Sokol’s list said otherwise. Lieb was at the flats over Lipsky’s at ten and Sokol’s at eleven. Miss Lowenthal and Sokol said so. Miss Kahane was at the flats over Lipsky’s at ten and Sokol’s at eleven; Miss Lowenthal and Sokol said so. Belkin hadn’t told me where he was at ten or eleven. Nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Fishel, the bookmaker at Sokol’s at twelve.
card: It was the middle of the night and the middle of the job, and neither one felt like an end.

before: I found Brennan at the far end, where the light gave up, and stood where he could see me without having to want to. “Weisglass has you at Moe’s at nine. Where were you the rest of the evening? All of it, in order.” ¶ He put down what he was holding and gave me his attention. ¶ “At eight I went round to Mrs. Nagy’s to return a borrowed umbrella, with Mrs. Bidwell. Come nine, I stopped in at Moe’s to get warm, with Sirkin. Around ten I went to the Eagle club office to write letters. At eleven I went to Moe’s to settle a bet. At ten and eleven I was on my own.” ¶ He said Moe’s at eleven, but Weisglass had Kreuzer, Sirkin and Lou at Moe’s at eleven o’clock, and nobody else. The rest of Brennan’s evening held where I could check it: Mrs. Bidwell had him at Mrs. Nagy’s at eight. ¶ One of those folded hands came unfolded, did something small, and went back. I’ve seen banks spend less carefully. ¶ The Turn: The Story Comes Apart ¶ I stopped where I was and went over it again, slowly, the way you reread a letter from the bank. ¶ Here’s what I had. Prentiss had said ten or eleven, and at ten Caruso was at Mrs. Nagy’s. Brennan, Sirkin and Quill were at Moe’s while Prentiss told the room. Kreuzer wasn’t. Brennan had told me Moe’s at eleven, and Weisglass’s list said otherwise. Kreuzer was at Mrs. Nagy’s at ten and Moe’s at eleven. Mrs. Bidwell and Weisglass said so. Sirkin was at Moe’s at ten and eleven; Weisglass said so. Quill hadn’t told me where he was at ten or eleven. Nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Lou at Moe’s at twelve. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to get over to Quill’s flat.
card: That was everything I had. It wasn’t enough yet.

before: Amato had said Miss Kahane was with him here at eight. That was reason enough to ask. She was handing a leaflet to somebody who already had two. She had a cardboard suitcase of leaflets she carries everywhere, held shut with a belt. ¶ I asked her where she’d been tonight. All of it, in order. ¶ She said she would tell me once, and I’d better be listening. ¶ “Where was I. I’ll tell you, and I’ll tell you straight, which is more than the police ever got out of a boss. I was at the Peacock at eight, with Amato. At nine I went up to the costume room at the Lyric to see the last act. Ten o’clock I went to the Peacock to dance. Then at eleven I went back to the costume room at the Lyric after all. Eleven, I write tomorrow’s speech. Every speech is the same speech. It’s still true. Nobody was with me at nine, ten or eleven.” ¶ She said the Peacock at ten, but Mrs. Szabo had Glick, Amato and Miss Marsh here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. ¶ Counting union dues into a cocoa tin: that was the last I saw of Miss Kahane. ¶ The Turn: Somebody Wasn’t There ¶ I stopped and took stock. Something had come loose, and I wanted to see what it was fastened to. ¶ Here’s what I had. Kaminsky had said nine or ten, and at nine Fritz was at Rafferty’s. Amato, Miss Kahane and Dr. Hirsch were at the Peacock while Kaminsky told the room. Glick wasn’t. Glick was at Rafferty’s at nine and the Peacock at ten; Miss Nowak and Mrs. Szabo said so. Amato was at the Peacock at nine and ten. Mrs. Szabo said so. Miss Kahane had told me the Peacock at ten, and Mrs. Szabo’s list said otherwise. Dr. Hirsch was at the Peacock at nine. Mrs. Szabo said so. And whatever it was had gone to Marsh, the cigarette girl at the Peacock at eleven. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to get over to the costume room at the Lyric.
card: That was the night so far: a lot of people who were somewhere, and one hour nobody wanted to talk about.

before: Ainsworth’s list had Ruggiero here at nine and eleven, so that was where I went next. ¶ I took the stool next to Ruggiero. I asked her for her evening, in order, the way you’d ask for a receipt. ¶ She gave it to me in as few words as the evening would go into. ¶ “I was at Doyle’s at eight, for the christening supper, with Colquitt. Nine o’clock I left the christening supper early and went to the Kit Kat to dance, and stayed the rest of the evening. Colquitt and Weisglass were there at nine; at ten it was just me; Colquitt and Weisglass were there at eleven.” ¶ She said the Kit Kat at ten, but Ainsworth had Colquitt, Weisglass and Lou here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. ¶ I wrote it down and underlined nothing. It was too early to underline. ¶ The Turn: Not Where They Said ¶ I leaned on the wall for a minute. The wall didn’t mind, and I needed the company. ¶ Here’s what I had. She went at nine or ten o’clock, and I didn’t know which yet. Ruggiero had told me the Kit Kat at ten, and Ainsworth’s list said otherwise. Ainsworth had Colquitt and Weisglass at the Kit Kat at nine and ten. Marchetti hadn’t told me where she was at nine or ten. Nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Lou at the Kit Kat at eleven. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to go over the parlor.
card: That was the night so far: a lot of people who were somewhere. One hour nobody wanted to talk about.

before: There was a pot of tea stewing on the back of the stove at all hours, offered to everybody, and always too strong to refuse politely. ¶ I asked Mrs. Rafferty who’d been in tonight, everybody, hour by hour. She started at the top of the evening and went down it like a column of figures. ¶ “Eight, I’ve the tea on and a sock on the egg and one ear on the door. Eight o’clock, nobody but me. Nine, Miss Moskin, and nobody else. Ten and eleven, nobody but me.” ¶ Miss Nowak said home at ten, but Mrs. Rafferty had nobody here at ten o’clock. ¶ I wrote it down. A watcher’s list is the one story in this city that nobody bothers to lie about. ¶ The Turn: An Hour Gone Missing ¶ I found a doorway and stood in it, and let the whole night go past me again, in order. ¶ Here’s what I had. She went at ten o’clock. Miss Kahane, Miss Moskin and Miss Nowak were at the supper and knew the way in. Glick wasn’t. Demos had Miss Kahane and Glick at Steinmetz’s at ten. Miss Nowak had told me home at ten, and Mrs. Rafferty’s list said otherwise. Miss Moskin hadn’t told me where she was at ten. Nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Tierney, the oyster opener at Steinmetz’s at eleven. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out what Miss Moskin had to say for herself.
card: Some of it would hold and some of it wouldn’t. I didn’t know yet which was which.

before: Pinsky’s list had Mrs. Sobel here at eight. I wanted the rest of it in her own words. ¶ She was telling somebody what they weighed at birth. She had spectacles on a chain, and a face that has seen everybody on Orchard Street at their very first and is not impressed by their since. I asked her where she’d been tonight, and who with, hour by hour. ¶ She answered straight off, the way people do with an evening they’ve only just finished. ¶ “You want to know where I was? Pull up a chair. It’s not a short story; I’m an old woman. I was at the Lyric at eight, with Glick. Come nine, I went home, with Mabry and Miss Lowenthal. Around ten I went round to the back booth at Sokol’s to see a man about a horse. Ten, I think about my late husband, may he rest. He’s resting. He was always good at it. At eleven I went to the Lyric, because a friend was in the show. Nobody was with me at ten or eleven.” ¶ She said the Lyric at eleven, but Pinsky had Glick, Mabry and Mrs. Shapiro here at eleven o’clock, and nobody else. ¶ Drinking tea from a glass with a lump of sugar in her teeth: that was the last I saw of her. ¶ The Turn: The One Who Lied ¶ I found a doorway and stood in it, and let the whole night go past me again, in order. ¶ Here’s what I had. Mrs. Blau had said ten or eleven, and at ten Mimi was at the flats over Lipsky’s. Mrs. Pomerantz, Glick and Mrs. Sobel were at the Lyric while Mrs. Blau told the room. Mabry wasn’t. Glick was at the Lyric at ten and eleven; Pinsky said so. Mabry was at the flats over Lipsky’s at ten and the Lyric at eleven. Miss Lowenthal and Pinsky said so. Mrs. Sobel had told me the Lyric at eleven, and Pinsky’s list said otherwise. Mrs. Pomerantz hadn’t told me where she was at ten or eleven. Nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Shapiro, the wardrobe mistress at the Lyric at twelve.
card: Some of it would hold and some of it wouldn’t. I didn’t know yet which was which.

before: Demos was folding napkins into shapes nobody asked for. “Who was in tonight?” I said. “All of them, hour by hour, and who you didn’t know.” ¶ He started at the top of the evening and went down it like a column of figures. ¶ “Eight, the full room, and one stands at the stand like a traffic policeman in a tailcoat. Tierney the oyster opener was there all evening, every hour of it. Eight o’clock, Glick, and nobody else that hour. Nine, Miss Kahane, Glick and Miss Nowak, and nobody else. Ten, Miss Kahane and Glick, and nobody else at all. Eleven, Miss Kahane, Glick and Miss Moskin. No one else, sir. Not in my room. Not without my say-so. Eleven: somebody came in with something under a coat and went straight to Tierney, and it changed hands. I was watching the coat, not the face.” ¶ “Under the coat,” I said. “What was it?” ¶ “Something that didn’t care to be carried. It moved.” ¶ Miss Moskin said Steinmetz’s at ten, but he had Miss Kahane, Glick and Tierney here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. Whatever went out of the Belkin flat, something came in here under a coat at eleven and went to Tierney. ¶ Writing covers in the book at his stand: that was the last I saw of Demos. ¶ The Turn: An Hour Gone Missing ¶ I stopped where I was and went over it again, slowly, the way you reread a letter from the bank. ¶ Here’s what I had. She went at ten o’clock. Miss Kahane, Miss Moskin and Miss Nowak were at the supper and knew the way in. Glick wasn’t. Demos had Miss Kahane and Glick at Steinmetz’s at ten. Miss Moskin had told me Steinmetz’s at ten, and Demos’s list said otherwise. Miss Nowak hadn’t told me where she was at ten. Nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Tierney, the oyster opener at Steinmetz’s at eleven. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out from the landlady at Rafferty’s who’d been in.
