before: Kaminsky was skipping rope in the kitchen and ducking the light bulb on every turn. ¶ I asked him where he’d been tonight. All of it, in order. He answered straight off, the way people do with an evening they’ve only just finished. ¶ “Sure. I’ll go the distance. Ask what you want. I was at the Peacock at eight, with Doyle. Eight, I do my roadwork in my head. My legs are tired. My head’s fresh. Then at nine I went home to listen to the radio, and stayed the rest of the evening, by myself.” ¶ He said home at eleven, but Mrs. Greco passed him on East Houston Street at eleven. The rest of his evening held where I could check it: Mrs. Szabo had him at the Peacock at eight, with Doyle. ¶ Shadowboxing in a corner, very quietly, so as not to bother anybody: that was the last I saw of him. ¶ The Turn: Two Stories ¶ I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest. ¶ Here’s what I had. Russo had said ten or eleven, and at ten Fritz was at the flats over Lipsky’s. Belkin, Kaminsky and Doyle were at the Peacock while Russo told the room. Mrs. Greco wasn’t. Kaminsky had told me home at eleven, and Mrs. Greco’s story said otherwise. Doyle was at the Peacock at ten and eleven; Mrs. Szabo said so. Mrs. Greco was at the flats over Lipsky’s at ten and the Peacock at eleven; Miss Lowenthal and Mrs. Szabo said so. Belkin hadn’t told me where he was at ten or eleven. Nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Marsh, the cigarette girl at the Peacock at twelve. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to get over to the little room at Wexler’s.
card: That was the night so far: a lot of people who were somewhere. One hour nobody wanted to talk about.

before: Mabry had said he was here at ten, so I wanted Sokol’s count of the night: everybody, hour by hour. ¶ The barman counts the glasses onto a towel at closing, and when one is short he knows whose it was. “You’ve been here all night,” I said. “Who came in, and when?” ¶ Sokol counted it off on his fingers, and ran out of fingers before he ran out of night. ¶ “Eight’s the regulars. I pour before they ask. It saves them the strain. Fishel the bookmaker was there all evening, every hour of it. Eight o’clock, Miss Kahane, and nobody else. Nine and ten, Mrs. Pomerantz and Miss Kahane. That’s everybody. I counted the glasses twice. Eleven: somebody came in with something under a coat and went straight to Fishel, and it changed hands. I was watching the coat, not the face.” ¶ “What was under the coat?” ¶ “Something small. If I’d seen more, I’d say more.” ¶ Mabry said Sokol’s at ten, but Sokol had Mrs. Pomerantz, Miss Kahane and Fishel here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. Whatever went out of the Glick flat, something came in here under a coat at eleven and went to Fishel. ¶ It turned out she was at the far end of the bar, nursing something. ¶ Humming a song from the old country into a glass while he dried it: that was the last I saw of him. ¶ The Turn: Where the Story Broke ¶ I went over it once more, the way you go over a bill you know is wrong. ¶ Here’s what I had. It went at ten o’clock. Mrs. Pomerantz was at Sokol’s at ten; Sokol said so. Mabry had told me Sokol’s at ten, and Sokol’s list said otherwise. Mrs. Ostrow hadn’t told me where she was at ten. Nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Fishel, the bookmaker at Sokol’s at eleven. ¶ I could put it to Mabry now. Or I could find out first from the usher at the Lyric who’d been in.

before: I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Hauck. I sat down where she could see me, and didn’t hurry. ¶ “Tell me where you were tonight,” I said. “Every hour, and anybody who can say so.” ¶ She thought for a second, the way anybody does, and started at the beginning. ¶ “I was at Bledsoe’s at eight, for the christening supper, with Feldman and Quill. Come nine, I left the christening supper early and had a ticket for the Thalia, with Feldman, Quill and Tramonti. Around ten I went to Moskowitz’s for a glass of tea, on my own.” ¶ She said Moskowitz’s at ten. Obermann says he was here at ten o’clock, with Feldman. They couldn’t both be true, and I knew which one I’d bet on. The rest of Hauck’s evening held where I could check it: Bledsoe had her at the Bledsoe flat at eight, with Quill. ¶ People always remember their own evenings well. It’s other people’s they go vague on. ¶ The Turn: The First Crack ¶ I found a doorway and stood in it, and let the whole night go past me again, in order. ¶ Here’s what I had. He went at ten o’clock. Feldman was at Moskowitz’s at ten; Obermann said so. Hauck had told me Moskowitz’s at ten, and Obermann’s story said otherwise. Quill hadn’t told me where she was at ten. Nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Benny at Moskowitz’s at eleven. ¶ I could put it to Hauck now. Or I could go over the parlor first.

before: I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Hochstetter. ¶ I went over to him and waited until he had a moment, which took a moment. “I need the whole night,” I said. “Everybody who was here, hour by hour, and anybody you didn’t know.” ¶ He answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Cheatham and Kessler, and nobody else. Eight and nine, Bernstein, Kessler and Sirkin, and nobody else at all. Ten, Ashby and Kessler, and nobody else that hour.” ¶ Cheatham said the Bijou at ten, but he had Ashby and Kessler here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. He had Kessler here at seven, same as she said.
card: I wrote it down in a column, one hour under the other. The way he’d said it.

before: Shapiro had said she was here all evening, so I wanted Kreuzer’s count of the night: everybody, hour by hour. ¶ Kreuzer saw me coming before I’d decided to come. That’s the job. I asked her for everybody she’d seen tonight, in order, and nobody left out because she liked them. ¶ She went through it the way you’d count change, carefully and out loud. ¶ “Eight o’clock, Feeney, Dandridge and Shapiro, and nobody else that hour. Nine, Dandridge and Shapiro, and nobody else. Ten, Abramowitz and Shapiro, and nobody else at all.” ¶ She had Abramowitz at ten, Feeney at eight and Shapiro at eight, same as they’d said. ¶ I still hadn’t looked properly at the floor at Dandridge’s place.
card: I wrote it down. Somebody whose job is watching a room doesn’t care who did what, only who came in, which makes them the best company in the city.

before: I sat down where Fairbanks could see me, and didn’t hurry. ¶ “Tell me where you were tonight,” I said. “Every hour, and anybody who can say so.” ¶ He told it the way you give somebody directions, landmark by landmark. ¶ “I was home at seven. Eight o’clock I went round to Rafferty’s to borrow a collar stud, with Shapiro. Then at nine I went home to change, and stayed the rest of the evening. I had nobody with me at seven, nine or ten.” ¶ He said home at ten. Rosenbaum passed him on Hester Street at ten. One of them was wrong.
